definition.stemRaw:
You are developing an application whose source repository has multiple branches. You have made several changes to a branch that is used for experimentation. You need to update the main branch so that it captures the changes made on the experimentation branch, while also overriding the history of the Git repository.  
  
Which Git option should you use?
definition.explanation:
Git rebase moves or replays the commits from one branch onto another, creating brand-new commits with new hashes for each original commit. This process rewrites the commit history, producing a linear sequence rather than preserving the original branching structure, which is what "overriding the history" refers to. Merge, by contrast, preserves the original history of both branches and adds a merge commit rather than rewriting it. Fetch only retrieves updates from a remote without integrating them, and Push only uploads local commits to a remote repository — neither operation integrates changes from another branch while rewriting history the way rebase does.

**Learn more:** [Merging vs. Rebasing | Atlassian Git Tutorial](https://www.atlassian.com/git/tutorials/merging-vs-rebasing) · [Git rebase | Atlassian Git Tutorial](https://www.atlassian.com/git/tutorials/rewriting-history/git-rebase)

finalExplanation: Git rebase moves or replays the commits from one branch onto another, creating brand-new commits with new hashes for each original commit. This process rewrites the commit history, producing a linear sequence rather than preserving the original branching structure, which is what "overriding the history" refers to. Merge, by contrast, preserves the original history of both branches and adds a merge commit rather than rewriting it. Fetch only retrieves updates from a remote without integrating them, and Push only uploads local commits to a remote repository — neither operation integrates changes from another branch while rewriting history the way rebase does.

You use Azure DevOps to build a web app named App1 and deploy App1 to VMSS1. App1 is used heavily and has usage patterns that vary on a weekly basis.  
  
You need to recommend a solution to detect an abnormal rise in the rate of failed requests to App1. The solution must minimize administrative effort.  
  
What should you include in the recommendation?

choices.label: B

definition.explanation:
Application Insights Smart Detection (Failure Anomalies) automatically monitors the rate of failed requests using machine learning and proactively alerts when there is an abnormal rise, without requiring you to author or maintain custom queries, thresholds, or alert rules. This built-in, automatic behavior satisfies the requirement to minimize administrative effort, whereas the Failures feature only provides manual investigation views, Azure Service Health covers Azure platform/service outages rather than app-level failures, and a custom Log Analytics-based alert would require ongoing manual query and threshold maintenance.

You need to configure a release pipeline that will mark the app as complete and ready for release into the Production-B environment. The solution must meet the following requirements:  
  
• Ensure that there are no active Azure Monitor alerts in the Production-A environment before the app is marked as complete.  

• Minimize administrative effort.  
  
What should you do?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To the Production-B environment stage, add a pre-deployment gate that will query Azure Monitor.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To the Production-A environment stage, add a post-deployment gate that will query Azure Monitor.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To the Production-A environment stage, add a post-deployment approval.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To the Production-A environment stage, add a pre-deployment gate that will query Azure Monitor.

definition.explanation: A post-deployment gate on the Production-A stage runs automatically after deployment completes and queries Azure Monitor for active alerts before Azure Pipelines marks that stage as successfully completed, which is the trigger for the pipeline to proceed toward Production-B. A pre-deployment gate on Production-B would check alerts before deploying to B rather than before Production-A is marked complete, and a manual approval doesn't automatically query Azure Monitor.

definition.stemRaw:
You have a web application hosted on Azure App Service that stores its data in an Azure SQL database.  
  
You need to generate an alert whenever there are 10,000 simultaneous connections to the database. The solution must minimize development effort.  
  
Which option should you select in the Diagnostics settings of the database?
definition.explanation:
Sending diagnostic data to Log Analytics lets you use Azure Monitor's built-in log search alert rules to evaluate collected metrics (such as connection counts) and trigger notifications automatically, requiring no custom code. Streaming to an Event Hub would require building and maintaining a separate consumer application to process the stream and raise alerts, increasing development effort. Archiving to a storage account only retains diagnostic data for later analysis and does not support real-time alerting. Therefore, routing the diagnostic logs to Log Analytics is the lowest-effort way to configure an alert for a threshold like 10,000 simultaneous connections.

**Learn more:** [Tutorial: Alert on Log Analytics data - Azure Monitor](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/alerts/tutorial-log-alert) · [Overview of Azure platform logs and diagnostic settings](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/essentials/diagnostic-settings)

finalExplanation: Sending diagnostic data to Log Analytics lets you use Azure Monitor's built-in log search alert rules to evaluate collected metrics (such as connection counts) and trigger notifications automatically, requiring no custom code. Streaming to an Event Hub would require building and maintaining a separate consumer application to process the stream and raise alerts, increasing development effort. Archiving to a storage account only retains diagnostic data for later analysis and does not support real-time alerting. Therefore, routing the diagnostic logs to Log Analytics is the lowest-effort way to configure an alert for a threshold like 10,000 simultaneous connections.

Your company has a release pipeline defined in an Azure DevOps project. You plan to deploy to an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster by using the Helm package and deploy task.  
  
You need to install a service in the AKS namespace to support the planned deployment.  
  
Which service should you install?
definition.explanation:
Helm v2 uses a client-server model where the Helm CLI communicates with a server-side component called Tiller that runs inside the Kubernetes cluster. Before Helm can package, install, or upgrade charts through the Azure DevOps Helm deploy task, Tiller must be installed into the target namespace (typically via 'helm init'), as it is responsible for executing the actual release operations against the Kubernetes API. Azure Container Registry is merely an external registry for storing images/charts, Chart is just the packaging artifact, and Kubectl is a command-line client rather than an in-cluster service, so none of those fulfill the requirement of an installable service within the AKS namespace.

**Learn more:** [Helm install (Helm 2 Tiller architecture)](https://v2.helm.sh/docs/install/)

Before Helm can package, install, or upgrade charts through the Azure DevOps Helm deploy task, Tiller must be installed into the target namespace (typically via 'helm init'), as it is responsible for executing the actual release operations against the Kubernetes API. Azure Container Registry is merely an external registry for storing images/charts, Chart is just the packaging artifact, and Kubectl is a command-line client rather than an in-cluster service, so none of those fulfill the requirement of an installable service within the AKS namespace.

You have an Azure DevOps organization named Contoso that contains a project named Project1. You also have an Azure subscription named Sub1 that includes an Azure key vault named vault1.  
  
You need to ensure that you can reference the values of the secrets stored in vault1 from all the pipelines in Project1. The solution must prevent the secret values from being stored in the pipelines.  
  
What should you do?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create a variable group in Project1.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add a secure file to Project1.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Modify the security settings of the pipelines.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Configure the security policy of Contoso.

finalExplanation: Azure Pipelines lets you create a variable group in the project's Library and link it to an existing Azure key vault. When you link the variable group to Key Vault, only the secret names are stored in the variable group definition; the actual secret values are retrieved directly from Key Vault at pipeline run time via an authorized service connection with Get and List permissions. A variable group can be made available to all pipelines in the project, satisfying the requirement to reference vault1's secrets from every pipeline in Project1 while ensuring the secret values themselves are never persisted in the pipeline definitions.

You use Git for source control. You have an app named App1.  
  
In the main branch, you need to restore the third most recent revision of a file named App.exe.config.  
  
How should you complete the command?
definition.template:
git {{b1}} main

git restore {{b2}} main~3 App.exe.config
definition.explanation:
To restore a file to the state it had at a prior commit, first ensure you are on the correct branch using git checkout main, then use git restore --source=<commit> <file> to pull the file's content from that specific commit into the working directory. The tree-ish main~3 refers to the commit three revisions back from the tip of main, which corresponds to the third most recent revision. The --source option is specifically designed to specify which commit to restore the file's content from, unlike --staged (which affects the index/staging area) or --patch/--merge (which serve different purposes in conflict resolution and interactive restoring).

**Learn more:** [git-restore Documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-restore)

The tree-ish main~3 refers to the commit three revisions back from the tip of main, which corresponds to the third most recent revision. The --source option is specifically designed to specify which commit to restore the file's content from, unlike --staged (which affects the index/staging area) or --patch/--merge (which serve different purposes in conflict resolution and interactive restoring).

You have an Azure Repos repository named `repo1`.  
  
You delete a branch named `features/feature11`.  
  
You need to recover the deleted branch.  
  
Which three commands should you run, in sequence?
definition.explanation:
A deleted branch is recovered by identifying its final commit, checking out that commit, and recreating the branch name at the current commit. `git log` displays commit history, `git checkout <SHA1>` selects the commit, and `git branch features/feature11` creates the branch there. `git restore` restores file contents and `git stash` saves uncommitted changes; neither recreates a branch.

**Learn more:** [Git - git-log Documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-log) · [Git - git-checkout Documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-checkout)

finalExplanation: A deleted branch is recovered by identifying its final commit, checking out that commit, and recreating the branch name at the current commit. `git log` displays commit history, `git checkout <SHA1>` selects the commit, and `git branch features/feature11` creates the branch there. `git restore` restores file contents and `git stash` saves uncommitted changes; neither recreates a branch.

definition.stemRaw: How should you configure the release retention policy for the investment planning applications suite?

blanks.label: Global release:
blanks.answer: Set the default retention policy to 30 days.
options: Set the default retention policy to 30 days.
Set the maximum retention policy to 30 days.
Set the stage retention policy to 30 days.
Set the stage retention policy to 60 days.

blanks.label: Production stage:
blanks.answer: Set the stage retention policy to 60 days.
options: Set the default retention policy to 30 days.
Set the maximum retention policy to 60 days.
Set the stage retention policy to 30 days.
Set the stage retention policy to 60 days.

finalExplanation: The investment planning applications suite requires that, by default, all releases remain available for 30 days, except for production releases, which must be kept for 60 days. In Azure DevOps classic release pipelines, the global (project-level) release retention settings include a Default retention policy, which sets the baseline number of days a release is retained for all release pipelines unless explicitly overridden - this satisfies the 30-day default requirement. Individual release pipelines can then customize a stage-specific retention policy (Days to retain a release) to extend retention for releases deployed to a particular stage, such as Production, beyond the global default - setting this to 60 days satisfies the requirement that production releases be kept longer. This two-tier retention model (global default plus per-stage override) is the documented mechanism for retaining production releases longer than non-production releases.

definition.stemRaw:
You manage an Azure web app that supports an e-commerce website.  
  
You need to increase the logging level when the web app exceeds normal usage patterns. The solution must minimize administrative overhead.  
  
Which two resources should you include in the solution? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.  
  
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

choices.label: B
choices.text: an Azure Monitor alert that has a dynamic threshold

choices.label: C
choices.text: an Azure Monitor alert that has a static threshold

choices.label: E
choices.text: an Azure Monitor alert that uses an action group that has an email action

definition.explanation:
Detecting when usage deviates from 'normal patterns' requires a dynamic threshold alert, which uses machine learning to establish a baseline from historical data and trigger only on anomalous deviations, rather than a fixed static threshold. To minimize administrative overhead, the response to that alert—raising the logging level—must happen automatically rather than relying on a person to read an email and make the change manually. An Azure Automation runbook can be configured as the alert's action to automatically execute the required change (e.g., updating diagnostic/logging settings) whenever the dynamic threshold alert fires.

**Learn more:** [Dynamic thresholds in metric alerts - Azure Monitor](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/alerts/alerts-dynamic-thresholds) · [Action groups - Azure Monitor](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/alerts/action-groups)

finalExplanation: Detecting when usage deviates from 'normal patterns' requires a dynamic threshold alert, which uses machine learning to establish a baseline from historical data and trigger only on anomalous deviations, rather than a fixed static threshold. To minimize administrative overhead, the response to that alert—raising the logging level—must happen automatically rather than relying on a person to read an email and make the change manually. An Azure Automation runbook can be configured as the alert's action to automatically execute the required change (e.g., updating diagnostic/logging settings) whenever the dynamic threshold alert fires.

definition.stemRaw:
You manage the Git repository for a large enterprise application. During development you use a file named Config.json. You need to prevent Config.json from being committed to source control whenever changes to the application are committed.  
  
Which three actions should you perform in sequence? Move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
items: Run the git reflog expire command.
definition.explanation:
Git uses a .gitignore file to specify files and patterns that should never be tracked or committed. The correct workflow is: first add the filename (Config.json) to the .gitignore file to define the ignore rule; then stage the .gitignore file itself with 'git add .gitignore' so the rule is tracked in the repository; finally commit that change with 'git commit' so the ignore rule takes effect for all future commits. Deleting and recreating the repository is destructive and unnecessary, and 'git reflog expire' only manages reference log history, not file tracking.

**Learn more:** [gitignore Documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/gitignore) · [Ignoring files - GitHub Docs](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/getting-started-with-git/ignoring-files)

finalExplanation: Git uses a .gitignore file to specify files and patterns that should never be tracked or committed. The correct workflow is: first add the filename (Config.json) to the .gitignore file to define the ignore rule; then stage the .gitignore file itself with 'git add .gitignore' so the rule is tracked in the repository; finally commit that change with 'git commit' so the ignore rule takes effect for all future commits. Deleting and recreating the repository is destructive and unnecessary, and 'git reflog expire' only manages reference log history, not file tracking.

definition.stemRaw:
You provision an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster with RBAC enabled. You have a Helm chart for a client application.  
  
You need to configure Helm and Tiller on the cluster and install the chart.  
  
Which three commands should you recommend running in sequence? Move the appropriate commands from the list of commands to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
definition.explanation:
On an RBAC-enabled AKS cluster, Tiller cannot operate with default permissions, so you must first create a dedicated service account and a ClusterRoleBinding for it using kubectl create (applying an RBAC manifest). Next, you run helm init --service-account tiller to initialize the Helm client and deploy Tiller into the cluster using that authorized service account. Finally, helm install is used to deploy the chart for the client application now that Tiller has the necessary permissions to create Kubernetes resources.

**Learn more:** [Role-based Access Control - Helm v2 Docs](https://v2.helm.sh/docs/rbac/) · [Install Tiller - Helm v2 Docs](https://v2.helm.sh/docs/using_helm/)

finalExplanation: On an RBAC-enabled AKS cluster, Tiller cannot operate with default permissions, so you must first create a dedicated service account and a ClusterRoleBinding for it using kubectl create (applying an RBAC manifest). Next, you run helm init --service-account tiller to initialize the Helm client and deploy Tiller into the cluster using that authorized service account. Finally, helm install is used to deploy the chart for the client application now that Tiller has the necessary permissions to create Kubernetes resources.

**Learn more:** [Publishing Docker images](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/tutorials/publish-packages/publish-docker-images) · [Working with the Container registry](https://docs.github.com/en/packages/working-with-a-github-packages-registry/working-with-the-container-registry)

Does this satisfy the goal?

Time between re-evaluation of gates controls how often gates are sampled; it does not control the timeout for a manual approval. An unapproved deployment is rejected when the approval Timeout period expires, so the approval timeout must be set to eight hours to meet the requirement.

Does this achieve the goal?
definition.explanation:
The gate re-evaluation interval only determines how often automated deployment gates are sampled. A pending manual approval is rejected when its configured approval timeout expires, so the approval timeout—not the post-deployment gate sampling interval—must be set to eight hours.

**Learn more:** [Deployment gates concepts - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/approvals/gates?view=azure-devops) · [Control deployments with release approvals - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/approvals/approvals?view=azure-devops)

definition.stemRaw:
Solution: In **Pre-deployment conditions**, modify the **Timeout** setting for pre-deployment approvals.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
definition.explanation:
The pre-deployment approval Timeout determines the period Azure DevOps waits for approval; if no approval is granted within that period, the deployment is rejected. Configuring it for eight hours ensures an unapproved deployment does not fail after two hours and is rejected only after the required eight-hour approval period.

**Learn more:** [Control deployments with release approvals - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/approvals/approvals?view=azure-devops)

finalExplanation: The pre-deployment approval Timeout determines the period Azure DevOps waits for approval; if no approval is granted within that period, the deployment is rejected. Configuring it for eight hours ensures an unapproved deployment does not fail after two hours and is rejected only after the required eight-hour approval period.

Does this achieve the goal?
definition.explanation:
A post-deployment approval occurs after the deployment, whereas the required team-leader approval must be completed before deployment. Its timeout therefore cannot control how long the deployment waits for that required approval. The pre-deployment approval timeout must be set to eight hours; when no approval is granted within that timeout, the deployment is rejected.

**Learn more:** [Control deployments with release approvals - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/approvals/approvals?view=azure-devops)

The pre-deployment approval timeout must be set to eight hours; when no approval is granted within that timeout, the deployment is rejected.

In an Azure DevOps project, a branch policy is configured that requires code to always build successfully before changes can be merged.

Branch policies such as requiring a successful build can be overridden by users granted the "Bypass policies when completing pull requests" (or "Bypass policies when pushing") permission. You have a private project in Azure DevOps.  
  
You need to ensure that a project manager can create custom work item queries to report on the project's progress. The solution must apply the principle of least privilege.  
  
To which security group should you add the project manager?

finalExplanation: By default in Azure DevOps, members of the Readers group can only view and run existing queries — they cannot create or save new ones. Members of the Contributors group, however, can create and save personal ('My Queries') custom work item queries by default, which is exactly what is needed to build reports on project progress. Project Administrators grant broader project-management capabilities (including creating/managing Shared Queries and folders, managing teams, area/iteration paths, repositories, and service endpoints), and Project Collection Administrators grant organization/collection-wide administrative rights across multiple projects — both exceed what is required for simply authoring custom queries. Therefore, adding the project manager to the Contributors group provides the minimum permissions necessary to accomplish the task, in line with the principle of least privilege.

choices.text: an Azure virtual machine scale set

finalExplanation: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents are self-hosted agents that Azure Pipelines can automatically scale out and in based on job demand. You can configure the number of agents to keep on standby down to 0, so Azure Pipelines only provisions a VM when a pipeline job is queued and removes idle agents after a configurable delay. This elasticity means you avoid paying for compute that sits idle nearly all day, which is ideal for a pipeline that only runs once daily for 30 minutes. This is explicitly the scenario Microsoft documentation calls out: 'You don't want to run dedicated agents around the clock. You want to de-provision agent machines that aren't being used to run jobs.' Standalone Azure VMs would require manual management to avoid idle costs, and AKS/Azure Container Instances are not the natively integrated, cost-optimized self-hosted agent scaling mechanism for this infrequent workload pattern.

You have an Azure solution that includes a build pipeline configured in Azure Pipelines.  
  
You notice that the build pipeline experiences intermittent delays before it starts running.  
  
You need to reduce the time it takes for the build pipeline to start.  
  
What should you do?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Split the build pipeline into multiple stages.

definition.explanation:
Azure Pipelines uses a limited number of parallel jobs (concurrent pipeline runs) per organization. When all available parallel jobs are in use, additional pipeline runs must queue and wait for a slot to free up, which produces intermittent start-up delays that vary with current load. Purchasing an additional parallel job increases the pool's run concurrency, allowing pipelines to start sooner instead of waiting in the queue. This is the documented mitigation from Microsoft's guidance on parallel jobs and pipeline queue times, as opposed to agent pool creation, self-hosted agent enablement (which addresses execution capacity/customization, not necessarily queue wait unless capacity is scaled), or splitting into stages (which restructures the pipeline but doesn't change queue wait time).

**Learn more:** [Parallel jobs in Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/licensing/concurrent-jobs)

finalExplanation: Azure Pipelines uses a limited number of parallel jobs (concurrent pipeline runs) per organization. When all available parallel jobs are in use, additional pipeline runs must queue and wait for a slot to free up, which produces intermittent start-up delays that vary with current load. Purchasing an additional parallel job increases the pool's run concurrency, allowing pipelines to start sooner instead of waiting in the queue. This is the documented mitigation from Microsoft's guidance on parallel jobs and pipeline queue times, as opposed to agent pool creation, self-hosted agent enablement (which addresses execution capacity/customization, not necessarily queue wait unless capacity is scaled), or splitting into stages (which restructures the pipeline but doesn't change queue wait time).

definition.stemRaw: Your company uses a Git source-code repository and you plan to implement GitFlow as a workflow strategy. You need to identify which branch type is used for production code and which is used for preproduction code in this strategy.
definition.explanation:
GitFlow defines two long-lived branches: main (master), which always contains production-ready, released code, and develop, which acts as the integration branch for features and represents the preproduction (next-release) state of the code. Feature branches are short-lived and used only to develop individual features before merging into develop, so they do not represent either production or preproduction code states.

You need to configure a cloud service to store the secrets required by the mobile applications to call the share pricing service.  
  
What should you include in the solution?

finalExplanation: In this case study, the legacy retirement fund management system's share pricing service will only support basic authentication over HTTPS until it is upgraded. Basic authentication requires credentials in the form of a username and password, which are Base64-encoded and sent in the HTTP Authorization header on each request — unlike certificates, personal access tokens, or Shared Access Authorization (SAS) tokens, which apply to different authentication mechanisms not used by this legacy service. To keep these credentials secure and centrally managed for the mobile applications, they should be stored in Azure Key Vault, which is designed specifically for storing and controlling access to secrets, keys, and certificates, reducing the risk of secrets being hard-coded or leaked in application code. Azure Data Lake and Azure Storage (whether accessed over HTTP or HTTPS) are data storage services and are not appropriate or secure locations for storing application secrets.

You have a web app named App1 that is hosted on multiple servers. App1 uses Application Insights in Azure Monitor.  
  
You need to compare the daily CPU usage from the last week for all servers.  
  
How should you complete the query? Each value may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

...
performanceCounters
| where counter == "% Processor Time"
| where timestamp >= ago(7d)
| summarize avg(value) by cloud_RoleInstance, {{time_bin}}
| {{render}}
...
definition.explanation:
`bin(timestamp,1d)` groups performance-counter samples into daily intervals while preserving `cloud_RoleInstance`, so average CPU is calculated separately for each server each day. `render timechart` renders the timestamped series as a time chart.

definition.stemRaw:
Your organization relies on Azure DevOps to handle the build pipelines and deployment pipelines for Java-based projects.  
  
You need to recommend a strategy for managing technical debt.  
  
Which two actions should be part of your recommendation? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.  
  
*(Choose two. Each correct selection is worth one point.)*

choices.label: A
choices.text: Configure post-deployment approvals in the deployment pipeline.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Configure pre-deployment approvals in the deployment pipeline.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Integrate Azure DevOps and Azure DevTest Labs.

finalExplanation: Technical debt in Java codebases is tracked using SonarQube's static code analysis, which measures code smells, bugs, vulnerabilities, duplications, and test coverage. Integrating Azure DevOps with SonarQube (via the SonarQube/SonarCloud marketplace extension) adds build tasks such as Prepare Analysis Configuration, Run Code Analysis, and Publish Quality Gate Result, which compute and publish a Quality Gate status for each build. To stop code that carries excessive technical debt from being promoted, that Quality Gate status is checked as a pre-deployment condition/gate on the release pipeline stage — the deployment pauses until the SonarQube Quality Gate check passes (or an approver intervenes), preventing poor-quality code from reaching downstream environments such as Production. Post-deployment approvals occur only after the deployment has already happened and therefore cannot block debt-laden code from being released, and Azure DevTest Labs is used for provisioning test/dev environments and has no role in measuring or gating on code quality/technical debt.

definition.stemRaw:
You need to recommend a Docker container build strategy that satisfies the following requirements:  
  
- Minimizes image sizes  
- Minimizes the security surface area of the final image  
  
What should you include in the recommendation?
definition.explanation:
Multi-stage builds let you use multiple FROM statements in a single Dockerfile, where earlier stages contain build tools, SDKs, and intermediate files, and only the final stage's necessary artifacts (such as compiled binaries) are copied into the final, minimal runtime image. This approach discards unneeded build dependencies and tools from the shipped image, directly reducing both the image size and the attack/security surface area, since fewer packages and tools are present that could be exploited. Docker's official documentation specifically recommends multi-stage builds for this purpose.

**Learn more:** [Multi-stage builds | Docker Docs](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/)

finalExplanation: Multi-stage builds let you use multiple FROM statements in a single Dockerfile, where earlier stages contain build tools, SDKs, and intermediate files, and only the final stage's necessary artifacts (such as compiled binaries) are copied into the final, minimal runtime image. This approach discards unneeded build dependencies and tools from the shipped image, directly reducing both the image size and the attack/security surface area, since fewer packages and tools are present that could be exploited. Docker's official documentation specifically recommends multi-stage builds for this purpose.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.text: Azure Resource Manager templates and the Custom Script Extension for Windows

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deployment YAML and Azure pipeline stage templates

finalExplanation: PowerShell Desired State Configuration (DSC) provides a declarative, idempotent way to define and enforce the configuration state of Windows machines, automatically correcting drift and maintaining consistency without ongoing manual intervention. Deploying the DSC extension through an Azure Resource Manager template lets the configuration be applied automatically as part of VM provisioning, satisfying both the consistency requirement and the goal of minimizing administrative effort. The Custom Script Extension only executes a script once and does not continuously enforce a desired state, and the YAML pipeline options (deployment groups/stage templates) are release orchestration constructs rather than configuration-state enforcement mechanisms.

definition.stemRaw: You have a project named Contoso App in Azure DevOps that contains pipelines in Azure Pipelines for GitHub repositories. You need to ensure that developers receive Microsoft Teams notifications when there are failures in a pipeline of Contoso App. What should you run in Teams?

You use Azure DevOps to manage the build and release process for an app named App1. A release pipeline deploys a virtual machine named VM1, and you plan to monitor the pipeline using Azure Monitor.  
  
You need to configure an alert rule to monitor VM1's performance. The alert must trigger when the average CPU usage exceeds 70 percent for a period of five minutes, and the average must be recalculated every minute.  
  
How should you configure the alert rule settings?

finalExplanation: In an Azure Monitor metric alert rule, the Aggregation granularity (Period) specifies the time window over which the metric values are aggregated for each evaluation; setting it to 5 minutes matches the requirement that the average CPU usage be evaluated over a five-minute span. The Threshold value must be Static because the alert uses a fixed, administrator-defined value (70 percent) rather than a value derived from machine-learning pattern analysis, which is what Dynamic thresholds use. The Operator must be Greater than because the condition specified is that CPU usage 'exceeds' 70 percent, which corresponds directly to a greater-than comparison rather than greater-than-or-equal, less-than, or less-than-or-equal. The separate 'Frequency of evaluation' setting (not shown in this set of options) would be set to 1 minute to satisfy the requirement that the average be recalculated every minute.

You have an Azure web app named webapp1 that uses the .NET Core runtime stack. You have an Azure Application Insights resource named AppInsights1 that collects telemetry data generated by webapp1.  
  
You plan to deploy webapp1 by using an Azure DevOps pipeline.  
  
You need to modify the sampling rate of the telemetry data processed by AppInsights1 without having to redeploy webapp1 after each modification.  
  
What should you do?

blanks.label: From the code repository of webapp1:
From AppInsights1:
blanks.answer: Modify the Usage and estimated costs settings.
options: Modify the Usage and estimated costs settings.

finalExplanation: Application Insights supports three sampling mechanisms: adaptive sampling, fixed-rate sampling, and ingestion sampling. Adaptive sampling is enabled by default in the ASP.NET Core SDK. Ingestion sampling operates at the Application Insights service endpoint and lets you set (and later change) the sampling percentage directly from the Azure portal, under Usage and estimated costs > Data Sampling, with no need to touch or redeploy the application. However, ingestion sampling is only honored when the SDK is not already performing adaptive or fixed-rate sampling - if the service endpoint detects telemetry already sampled below 100%, it ignores the configured ingestion sampling rate. Because webapp1 is a .NET Core app, adaptive sampling is active by default and must be disabled in the application code (in Program.cs/appsettings.json, since ApplicationInsights.config does not apply to the ASP.NET Core SDK). Once adaptive sampling is disabled, all subsequent sampling-rate changes can be made purely from AppInsights1's Usage and estimated costs pane in the Azure portal, without any further code changes or pipeline redeployments.

You are planning the release strategies for a new app. You need to choose a strategy for each of the following scenarios:

finalExplanation:
Progressive exposure (deployment rings) groups users by their tolerance for risk/faults, releasing new versions first to users with high fault tolerance and progressively expanding to broader, more risk-averse groups as confidence grows — this controls the 'blast radius' of a bad release.


Feature flags (feature toggles) let you deploy code to production while keeping new functionality hidden or disabled, so it can be enabled later in a future release without requiring a new deployment — this decouples deployment from release.


Blue/green deployment maintains two identical production environments (the 'blue' currently live one and the 'green' new one). Because the old (blue) environment remains fully active and untouched while the new version runs in green, traffic can be switched back instantly, minimizing recovery time if a rollback is needed.

definition.explanation:
In Kusto Query Language (KQL) used by Azure Monitor Log Analytics, the summarize operator groups rows by a specified key and applies an aggregation function to each group, using the syntax 'summarize <Aggregation> by <GroupExpression>'. To obtain only the distinct (non-duplicated) Event IDs recorded on each computer, the make_set()/makeset() aggregation function is required, since it creates a dynamic JSON array containing only the distinct values of the expression within each group — unlike makelist(), which preserves duplicates. Grouping by Computer produces one row per virtual machine, each containing the array of unique event IDs recorded on that machine within the last 12 hours, matching the requirement shown for VM1 and VM2 in the table.

**Learn more:** [make_set() (aggregation function) - Kusto](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/kusto/query/make-set-aggregation-function) · [summarize operator - Kusto](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/kusto/query/summarize-operator)

definition.stemRaw: You have an Azure Resource Manager template that deploys a multi-tier application. You need to prevent the user who performs the deployment from viewing the account credentials and connection strings used by the application. What should you use?

choices.label: E
choices.text: an Azure Resource Manager parameter file

finalExplanation: Azure Key Vault allows you to store secrets, such as account credentials and connection strings, and reference them in an ARM template parameter file using a static or dynamic Key Vault reference. When a parameter references a Key Vault secret, Azure Resource Manager retrieves the secret value securely at deployment time without exposing it in the template, deployment outputs, or deployment history to the person performing the deployment—unless that person is separately granted access to read the secret from the vault. This ensures credentials remain hidden from the deployer while still being usable by the deployment process. Configuration files like Web.config or appsettings.json store secrets in plaintext within the application, offering no protection against a deploying user viewing them, and Azure Storage tables and plain ARM parameter files (without Key Vault integration) also do not provide this secret-hiding capability.

The Release Pipeline Overview widget displays the current status of each environment/stage defined in a release pipeline, satisfying the requirement to monitor release environment status. finalExplanation: Azure Monitor action groups natively support a Logic App action type, enabling alerts to trigger a Logic App workflow without custom infrastructure. To set this up with minimal effort: first create an Azure Logic App, configure it to start with the 'HTTP request' (When a HTTP request is received) trigger so it can accept the alert payload, then update the existing action group in Azure Monitor to add this Logic App as an action. When the alert fires, Azure Monitor invokes the action group, which calls the Logic App via HTTP, and the Logic App can then transform and forward the error details to the third-party system. This avoids building custom event hub consumers or polling-based triggers such as Recurrence or Sliding Window, which are unnecessary for an alert-driven push scenario.

Your organization has a project in Azure DevOps. You need to make sure that when several builds are pending deployment at the same time, only the most recent build actually gets deployed.  
  
What should you use to accomplish this?
definition.explanation:
Azure DevOps release pipelines let you configure, per stage, how queued deployments are processed via the Deployment queue settings. One of the available options, 'Deploy latest and cancel others,' automatically cancels or skips older queued releases and deploys only the most recent one when multiple releases are waiting for deployment to the same stage. This is exactly the mechanism designed to prevent outdated builds from being deployed after a newer build is already queued.

definition.explanation:

definition.stemRaw: To resolve the current technical issue, what should you do to the Register-AzureRmAutomationDscNode command?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Change the value of the ConfigurationMode parameter.

definition.explanation:
The Register-AzureRmAutomationDscNode cmdlet's ConfigurationMode parameter determines how Azure Automation State Configuration (DSC) applies and maintains a node's configuration. Setting it to ApplyOnly causes DSC to apply the configuration a single time and never check for or correct drift afterward, which is why previously correctly configured servers were drifting out of compliance over time. Changing the ConfigurationMode value to ApplyAndAutoCorrect causes DSC to periodically check the node against the desired configuration and automatically correct any detected drift, resolving the issue.

**Learn more:** [To resolve the current technical issue, what should you do to the Register-AzureRmAutomationDscNode command? - Exam4Training](https://www.exam4training.com/to-resolve-the-current-technical-issue-what-should-you-do-to-the-register-azurermautomationdscnode-command-11/)

Setting it to ApplyOnly causes DSC to apply the configuration a single time and never check for or correct drift afterward, which is why previously correctly configured servers were drifting out of compliance over time. Changing the ConfigurationMode value to ApplyAndAutoCorrect causes DSC to periodically check the node against the desired configuration and automatically correct any detected drift, resolving the issue.

You are configuring an alert rule in Azure Monitor for the ASP-9bb7 resource, as shown in the exhibit below.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783719579988-bthtqarc.jpg)  
  
Which action will cause this alert to fire?

choices.label: A
choices.text: a failed attempt to delete the ASP-9bb7 resource

choices.label: B
choices.text: a change to a role assignment for the ASP-9bb7 resource

choices.label: C
choices.text: a successful attempt to delete the ASP-9bb7 resource

choices.label: D
choices.text: a failed attempt to scale up the ASP-9bb7 resource

finalExplanation: The alert rule's condition is: Activity Log, Category='Administrative', Signal name='All Administrative operations', Status='failed'. The Administrative category in the Azure Activity Log records create, update, delete, and action operations performed through Azure Resource Manager, and both the start and the success/fail outcome of each such operation are logged. Because the rule's Status filter is set specifically to 'failed', only a failed administrative operation on ASP-9bb7 (such as a failed delete) satisfies the condition. A successful delete has Status='Succeeded' and does not match. Scale operations (whether manual or via autoscale) are logged under the distinct 'Autoscale' Activity Log category, not 'Administrative', so a failed scale-up attempt would not be captured by this rule. A role-assignment change is logged under Administrative but is not stated to have failed, so it does not reliably satisfy the Status='failed' requirement the way an explicitly failed delete attempt does.

You are creating a container for an ASP.NET Core app.  
  
You need to create a Dockerfile to build the image, ensuring the resulting image size is minimized.  
  
How should you configure the file? Each value may be used once, more than once, or not at all.
definition.template:
FROM {{from1}} AS build-env
COPY . /app/
WORKDIR /app
RUN {{run1}}
FROM {{from2}}
COPY --from=build-env /app/out /app
WORKDIR /app
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", " MvcMovie.dll"]

finalExplanation: Multi-stage Docker builds minimize final image size by separating the build environment from the runtime environment. The build stage uses the full SDK image (mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:5.0), which includes compilers and build tooling needed to compile and publish the application via 'dotnet publish -c Release -o out'. The final stage uses the much smaller ASP.NET Core runtime-only image (mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:5.0), which contains only what is needed to run the compiled app, not the SDK or build tools. Copying just the published output (COPY --from=build-env) into this lightweight runtime image ensures the shipped container is as small as possible, following Microsoft's documented .NET Docker multi-stage build guidance.

finalExplanation: In Azure Repos, a Build Validation policy queues a build pipeline against the proposed changes whenever a pull request is created or updated; if the build fails, the pull request cannot be completed, which directly enforces that committed code compiles successfully. A Status Check (status) policy allows a third-party or external service — such as SonarCloud — to post a pass/fail status to the pull request through the PR Status API; when configured as required, the PR cannot merge until that external status (e.g., 'SonarCloud/quality gate' = Passed) is reported as succeeded. definition.stemRaw:
You are designing a versioning strategy for Git-based packages, using a Semantic Versioning (SemVer)-based approach.  
  
You need to identify when to change the build version for each of the following scenarios. Each version may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

slots.label: You rename a parameter in an API:
You deprecate functionality in an API:
You add a feature and maintain backwards compatibility:

finalExplanation: Under Semantic Versioning (SemVer 2.0.0), the MAJOR version is incremented when incompatible (breaking) API changes are introduced; renaming a parameter breaks any existing code referencing that parameter name, so it requires a Major version change. The MINOR version is incremented when new backward-compatible functionality is added — 'You add a feature and maintain backwards compatibility' is the canonical example of a Minor release. The SemVer specification's own FAQ also states that when part of a public API is deprecated, the correct practice is to document the change and 'issue a new minor release with the deprecation in place' before removing the functionality entirely in a later Major release — since the deprecated feature still works and nothing breaks yet, this is a Minor change, not a Major one. Patch versions are reserved strictly for backward-compatible bug fixes, which none of these three scenarios describe.

definition.stemRaw:
You need to configure access to Azure DevOps agent pools to meet the following requirements:  
  
- Use a project agent pool when authoring build or release pipelines.  
- View the agent pool and agents of the organization.  
- Use the principle of least privilege.  
  
Which role memberships are required for the Azure DevOps organization and the project? Each role membership may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

finalExplanation:
Azure DevOps defines separate security roles at the organization level and the project level for agent pools.


At the organization level, the Reader role allows members to view the agent pool and agents — this satisfies the requirement to view the organization's agent pool and agents without granting the broader rights of the Service Account role (which allows creating a project agent pool from the organization pool) or the Administrator role (which allows registering/unregistering agents and managing role membership). Reader is therefore the least-privileged choice for this requirement.


At the project level, the User role allows members to use the project agent pool when authoring pipelines — this exactly satisfies the requirement to use a project agent pool when authoring build or release pipelines. The Administrator role at the project level additionally allows managing role membership, which is unnecessary and violates least privilege, so User is the correct minimal role.

definition.explanation:
The Azure Pipelines GitHub App is the recommended authentication mechanism for connecting Azure Pipelines to GitHub repositories. Once installed in the GitHub account or organization, it becomes the default authentication method for pipelines and causes builds and GitHub status updates to run under the dedicated Azure Pipelines service identity, rather than under the personal identity of the user who set up the connection. In contrast, both OAuth and personal access token (PAT) authentication tie the pipeline to the individual user's GitHub identity, meaning the pipeline could break if that user's access changes or is revoked. Azure AD is not applicable for this GitHub integration scenario. This makes the GitHub App the correct choice for ensuring pipeline runs use the Azure Pipelines identity.

finalExplanation: The Azure Pipelines GitHub App is the recommended authentication mechanism for connecting Azure Pipelines to GitHub repositories. Once installed in the GitHub account or organization, it becomes the default authentication method for pipelines and causes builds and GitHub status updates to run under the dedicated Azure Pipelines service identity, rather than under the personal identity of the user who set up the connection. In contrast, both OAuth and personal access token (PAT) authentication tie the pipeline to the individual user's GitHub identity, meaning the pipeline could break if that user's access changes or is revoked. Azure AD is not applicable for this GitHub integration scenario. This makes the GitHub App the correct choice for ensuring pipeline runs use the Azure Pipelines identity.

You need to deploy a workflow for repo1 by using GitHub Actions. The solution must meet the following requirements:  
  
- Scan on pushes to the main branch.  
- Scan on pull requests to the main branch.  
- Scan on pull requests to any branch that has a prefix of releases/.  
- Scan all the files in the subdirectories of the src directory.  
- Exclude scanning of markdown files.  
  
How should you complete the code? Each value may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

on:

  push:

    branches: [main]

  pull_request:

    branches:

  - main

  {{branches2}}

  paths:

  {{paths}}

  paths-ignore:

  {{pathsignore}}

...

finalExplanation: In GitHub Actions workflow trigger filters, glob patterns use double-asterisk (**) to match across directory levels, while single-asterisk (*) only matches within a single path segment. To trigger on pull requests to branches prefixed with 'releases/', the pattern 'releases/**' is required because it matches any branch name that begins with that prefix regardless of additional path segments (e.g., releases/2023, releases/2023/hotfix). For the paths filter, scanning all files within subdirectories of src requires 'src/**', since 'src/*' only matches files directly inside src and not nested subdirectories. For paths-ignore, excluding all markdown files anywhere in the repository (not just at the root) requires '**/*.md', because '*.md' only matches markdown files in the root directory. These glob semantics are documented in GitHub's workflow syntax reference for filtering branches and paths.

Your company deploys applications using Docker containers. You want to detect known exploits in the Docker images used to provision the Docker containers. You need to integrate image scanning into the application lifecycle, and the solution must expose the exploits as early as possible during the application lifecycle.  
  
What should you configure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: a task executed in the continuous integration pipeline and a scheduled task that analyzes the image registry

choices.label: B
choices.text: manual tasks performed during the planning phase and the deployment phase

choices.label: C
choices.text: a task executed in the continuous deployment pipeline and a scheduled task against a running production container

choices.label: D
choices.text: a task executed in the continuous integration pipeline and a scheduled task that analyzes the production container

definition.explanation:
Scanning images as part of the continuous integration pipeline detects known vulnerabilities at build time, which is the earliest possible point in the application lifecycle — before an image is ever pushed or deployed. Because new CVEs are discovered continuously after images are built, a scheduled task that re-analyzes the image registry ensures that images already stored (and possibly deployed) are re-evaluated against newly published vulnerability data, so exploits discovered after the initial CI scan are still detected. This combination (CI-time scanning plus ongoing registry scanning) provides both early detection and continuous coverage, which is the approach used by services such as Google Container Registry/Artifact Registry vulnerability scanning via the Container Analysis API.

**Learn more:** [Container Analysis - Scanning images for vulnerabilities](https://cloud.google.com/container-analysis/docs/container-scanning-overview)

finalExplanation: Scanning images as part of the continuous integration pipeline detects known vulnerabilities at build time, which is the earliest possible point in the application lifecycle — before an image is ever pushed or deployed. Because new CVEs are discovered continuously after images are built, a scheduled task that re-analyzes the image registry ensures that images already stored (and possibly deployed) are re-evaluated against newly published vulnerability data, so exploits discovered after the initial CI scan are still detected. This combination (CI-time scanning plus ongoing registry scanning) provides both early detection and continuous coverage, which is the approach used by services such as Google Container Registry/Artifact Registry vulnerability scanning via the Container Analysis API.

You have a containerized solution running in Azure Container Instances. The solution includes a frontend container named App1 and a backend container named DB1. DB1 loads a large amount of data during startup.

definition.explanation:
Azure Container Instances supports readiness probes, which determine whether a container is ready to accept incoming traffic. Until the readiness probe succeeds, the container is not considered available to serve requests, which is exactly what's needed to ensure DB1 has finished loading its startup data before App1 begins accepting user requests. A liveness probe only checks whether a running container should be restarted due to an unresponsive state and does not gate initial readiness; performance logs provide diagnostic data rather than traffic control; and Azure Load Balancer health probes apply to load balancer backend pools, not to container groups in Azure Container Instances.

**Learn more:** [Azure Container Instances - add liveness and readiness probes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-instances/container-instances-liveness-probe)

Until the readiness probe succeeds, the container is not considered available to serve requests, which is exactly what's needed to ensure DB1 has finished loading its startup data before App1 begins accepting user requests. A liveness probe only checks whether a running container should be restarted due to an unresponsive state and does not gate initial readiness; performance logs provide diagnostic data rather than traffic control; and Azure Load Balancer health probes apply to load balancer backend pools, not to container groups in Azure Container Instances.

Perf
| where {{time_filter}}
| where Computer == "web1"

finalExplanation: Azure Key Vault separates management (control plane) operations, such as deleting the vault, from data plane operations, such as reading secrets. Control plane operations, including delete access to the vault resource, are restricted using Azure role-based access control (RBAC) role assignments scoped to the Key Vault resource. Data plane access to the secrets themselves is restricted using a Key Vault access policy that grants only the specific permissions (e.g., Get/List on secrets) required by the release pipeline's service principal, satisfying least privilege. finalExplanation: Migrating a Git repository while preserving all branches, tags, and full history requires creating a bare (mirror) clone of the source repository and then pushing that bare clone with --mirror to the destination. git clone --bare downloads all refs (branches, tags) from the GitHub source without a working directory, creating a local folder named project1.git. Changing into that directory (cd project1.git) is required before pushing. Finally, git push --mirror to the Azure Repos URL pushes every ref exactly as it exists in the source, and because --mirror makes the destination an exact mirror of the source, the Azure Repos repository ends up containing only the branches and history that exist in the GitHub repository (overwriting/removing anything else that might already be there).

You need to recommend a solution to store and encrypt the secret. The secret value must be accessible only to the workflow. The solution must minimize administrative effort

choices.text: Store the secret in the organization-level GitHub secrets.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Store the secret in the repository-level GitHub secrets.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Encrypt the secret value and store the value in the repository. Store the decryption key in the repository-level GitHub secrets.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Encrypt the secret value and store the value in the repository. Store the decryption key in the organization-level GitHub secrets.

definition.explanation: GitHub Actions has a built-in 48-KB secret size limit. For secrets larger than 48 KB, the recommended approach is to encrypt the secret value yourself and store it in the repository, then store the decryption key in repository-level GitHub secrets. This way, the secret is encrypted at rest and only decryptable by the workflow using the key from the repo secrets, minimizing administrative overhead compared to organization-level management.

For secrets larger than 48 KB, the recommended approach is to encrypt the secret value yourself and store it in the repository, then store the decryption key in repository-level GitHub secrets. definition.stemRaw:
You have an app named App1 and a Log Analytics workspace named Workspace1. Workspace1 contains a table named AppEvents, and App1 writes logs to Workspace1.  
  
You need to query the AppEvents table. The solution must meet these requirements:  
  
- Query only rows where the **Name** column starts with "Clicked Create New Ticket."  
- Calculate daily clicks per user.  
- Return the top 10 users by their number of clicks on any day.  
- Sort the results by the highest click count.  
- Exclude users with fewer than three daily clicks.  
  
In which order should the query statements be arranged?

slots.answer: | where Name startswith "Clicked Create New Ticket
| summarize NumberOfClicks = count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 1d), UserId

items: | summarize NumberOfClicks = count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 1d), UserId
| where Name startswith "Clicked Create New Ticket
definition.explanation:
Kusto filters source rows with `where` before `summarize` aggregates them. Grouping `count()` by `bin(TimeGenerated, 1d)` and `UserId` produces each user’s daily click total. Filtering that aggregate to `NumberOfClicks >= 3` excludes lower totals, and `top 10 by NumberOfClicks desc` returns the ten largest totals in descending order.

**Learn more:** [where operator - Kusto](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/kusto/query/where-operator?view=microsoft-fabric) · [summarize operator - Kusto](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/kusto/query/summarize-operator?view=microsoft-fabric)

finalExplanation: Kusto filters source rows with `where` before `summarize` aggregates them. Grouping `count()` by `bin(TimeGenerated, 1d)` and `UserId` produces each user’s daily click total. Filtering that aggregate to `NumberOfClicks >= 3` excludes lower totals, and `top 10 by NumberOfClicks desc` returns the ten largest totals in descending order.

definition.stemRaw:
Your company has a project in Azure DevOps.  
  
You plan to create a release pipeline that will deploy resources by using Azure Resource Manager templates. The templates will reference secrets stored in Azure Key Vault.  
  
You need to recommend a solution for accessing the secrets stored in the key vault during deployments. The solution must use the principle of least privilege.  
  
What should you include in the recommendation? Each configuration may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

slots.label: Enable key vaults for template deployment by using:
slots.answer: A Key Vault advanced access policy

slots.label: Restrict access to the secrets in Key Vault by using:

items: A Key Vault advanced access policy

finalExplanation:
To let Azure Resource Manager retrieve secrets from a key vault during template deployment, the vault's enabledForTemplateDeployment property must be set to true. This setting is exposed in the Azure portal as an 'Advanced access policy' checkbox ('Enable access to Azure Resource Manager for template deployment') and can be set via Set-AzKeyVaultAccessPolicy -EnabledForTemplateDeployment or az keyvault update --enabled-for-template-deployment true.


Once template deployment is enabled on the vault, access to the individual secrets is still governed separately. To follow least privilege, you grant only the specific permissions needed (typically just Get on secrets) to the specific user, group, or service principal performing the deployment by configuring a standard Key Vault access policy (az keyvault set-policy / Set-AzKeyVaultAccessPolicy -PermissionsToSecrets), rather than granting broad Key Vault management permissions.

definition.stemRaw:
You manage an Azure DevOps project that contains package feeds.  
  
You need to make sure developers are able to unlist and deprecate packages, while adhering to the principle of least privilege.  
  
Which access level should you assign to the developers?
definition.explanation:
In Azure Artifacts, the Contributor role on a feed grants the ability to push, unlist, and deprecate packages, which is exactly the permission needed here. The Reader and Collaborator roles do not include rights to unlist or deprecate packages—Collaborator only adds the ability to save packages from upstream sources. The Owner role includes these capabilities too, but also grants full administrative control (deleting the feed, changing feed settings, managing permissions), which exceeds what is required and violates the principle of least privilege. Therefore, Contributor is the minimal role that satisfies the requirement.

**Learn more:** [Feed permissions - Azure Artifacts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/artifacts/feeds/feed-permissions)

finalExplanation: In Azure Artifacts, the Contributor role on a feed grants the ability to push, unlist, and deprecate packages, which is exactly the permission needed here. The Reader and Collaborator roles do not include rights to unlist or deprecate packages—Collaborator only adds the ability to save packages from upstream sources. The Owner role includes these capabilities too, but also grants full administrative control (deleting the feed, changing feed settings, managing permissions), which exceeds what is required and violates the principle of least privilege. Therefore, Contributor is the minimal role that satisfies the requirement.

You are configuring an Azure DevOps deployment pipeline. The deployed application will authenticate to a web service by using a secret stored in an Azure key vault.

Which three actions should you perform in sequence? Move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.

slots.answer: Create a service principal in Azure Active Directory (Azure AD).
Configure an access policy in the key vault.
Add an Azure Resource Manager service connection to the pipeline.

items: Create a service principal in Azure Active Directory (Azure AD).
Add an app registration in Azure Active Directory (Azure AD).
Configure an access policy in the key vault.
Add an Azure Resource Manager service connection to the pipeline.
Export a certificate from the key vault.

finalExplanation: Consuming a Key Vault secret from an Azure DevOps pipeline requires an Azure AD identity that the pipeline can use, permission for that identity to read the secret, and a way for the pipeline to authenticate as that identity. First, create a service principal in Azure AD to represent the pipeline's identity. Second, configure an access policy on the key vault granting that service principal Get/List permissions on secrets so it is authorized to retrieve them. Third, add an Azure Resource Manager service connection in the pipeline (backed by the service principal) so tasks such as the Azure Key Vault task can authenticate and pull the secret into the pipeline at deployment time. Creating an app registration, generating a self-signed certificate, or exporting a certificate from the vault are not required steps in this standard workflow.

definition.stemRaw:
Your company is building an iOS application, and every user of the app has a device that belongs to a private distribution group configured in Microsoft Visual Studio App Center.  
  
You are preparing to distribute a new release of the app through App Center.  
  
You need to determine which certificate file you must upload to App Center in order to distribute this new release.  
  
Which file type should you upload to App Center?
definition.explanation:
App Center's iOS distribution and device auto-provisioning process re-signs the app for devices registered in the distribution group, which requires the distribution certificate along with its private key. On macOS this certificate and key pair is exported from Keychain Access as a PKCS#12 container using the .p12 file extension, which is the file type App Center requires you to upload for iOS release management. A .cer file contains only the public certificate without the private key, .pfx is the Windows-style PKCS#12 extension not used in the Apple ecosystem, and .pvk is a separate private-key file format used with Microsoft's code-signing tools, none of which App Center accepts for this purpose.

**Learn more:** [Device registration - Visual Studio App Center | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/appcenter/distribution/auto-provisioning)

finalExplanation: App Center's iOS distribution and device auto-provisioning process re-signs the app for devices registered in the distribution group, which requires the distribution certificate along with its private key. On macOS this certificate and key pair is exported from Keychain Access as a PKCS#12 container using the .p12 file extension, which is the file type App Center requires you to upload for iOS release management. A .cer file contains only the public certificate without the private key, .pfx is the Windows-style PKCS#12 extension not used in the Apple ecosystem, and .pvk is a separate private-key file format used with Microsoft's code-signing tools, none of which App Center accepts for this purpose.

definition.stemRaw:
You are building a pipeline in Azure Pipelines. Several of the tests you have defined may fail because of the third-party applications they depend on. You need to make sure the build pipeline still completes successfully even when those third-party applications are unavailable.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Configure the build pipeline to use parallel jobs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add the Requirements quality widget to your dashboard

finalExplanation: Azure DevOps provides a flaky test management feature (enabled under Project Settings > Test management) specifically to handle tests that produce inconsistent pass/fail results due to factors outside the code itself, such as unreliable or unavailable third-party dependencies. Once a test is detected or manually marked as flaky, you can configure the flaky test options so that flaky test failures are excluded from the test summary/pass percentage and the failure is suppressed, allowing the overall pipeline to complete successfully instead of being marked as failed. This directly addresses failures caused by third-party application unavailability, unlike parallel jobs (which only affects execution speed/concurrency), raising the pass percentage threshold (which is a blunt, pipeline-wide tolerance setting not tied to identifying specific unreliable tests), or the Requirements quality dashboard widget (a reporting visualization with no effect on pipeline outcome).

definition.stemRaw: You manage the Git repository for a large enterprise application. You need to minimize the data size of the repository. How should you complete the commands?
definition.template:
git gc {{gc_opt}}
git {{cmd}} --expire now
definition.explanation:
Running 'git gc --aggressive' performs a more thorough repack and recompression of the object database, reducing repository size more than a standard 'git gc'. Following it with 'git prune --expire now' immediately removes all loose objects that are no longer reachable from any reference, without the default 2-week grace period, further shrinking the repository. Together these commands are the standard approach documented by Git for minimizing repository disk usage.

**Learn more:** [git-gc Documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-gc) · [git-prune Documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-prune)

Following it with 'git prune --expire now' immediately removes all loose objects that are no longer reachable from any reference, without the default 2-week grace period, further shrinking the repository. Together these commands are the standard approach documented by Git for minimizing repository disk usage.

You have an Azure DevOps project named Project1 and an Azure subscription named Sub1.  
  
You need to ensure that releases are not deployed unless they meet the Azure Policy rules assigned to Sub1.  
  
What should you configure in the release pipeline of Project1?
definition.explanation:
Deployment gates in Azure Pipelines let you add automated checks (such as a call to an Azure Function, Azure Monitor alert, or REST API) that must succeed before a release is allowed to proceed to a stage. By configuring a gate that queries Azure Policy compliance status for the target resources, you can block a release from being deployed until it satisfies the Azure Policy rules assigned to Sub1. Deployment queue settings only control how concurrent releases are queued, deployment triggers control when a release is created/started, and pipeline variables merely store configuration values—none of these enforce policy compliance checks before deployment.

Configure the DSC extension on the virtual machines.

items: Configure the DSC extension on the virtual machines.
Load the file to Azure Blob storage.
Configure the Custom Script Extension on the virtual machines.
Load the file to Azure Files.

finalExplanation: Azure PowerShell Desired State Configuration (DSC) requires a PowerShell configuration script (.ps1) that defines the desired state, such as ensuring a Windows feature is installed. This configuration is packaged (zipped) and published to an accessible location — Azure Blob storage is the standard and documented target used by cmdlets like Publish-AzVMDscConfiguration, which uploads the package and secures it with a SAS token. Finally, the DSC extension is configured on the virtual machines, pointing to the blob-stored configuration package so the VM Agent downloads and applies it, and continues to enforce that the specified Windows feature remains installed (self-correcting configuration drift). Using YAML, Custom Script Extension, or Azure Files does not align with how the Azure DSC extension is designed to operate.

You manage a build pipeline in Azure Pipelines that occasionally fails. You determine that a test which measures the response time of an API endpoint is the cause of these failures. You need to stop the build pipeline from failing because of this test.  
  
Which two actions should you take? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. (Choose two.)  
  
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Set Flaky test detection to Off.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clear Flaky tests included in test pass percentage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Manually mark the test as flaky.

finalExplanation: Azure Pipelines' flaky test management feature allows a specific test to be manually flagged as flaky, after which Azure DevOps continues to treat it as flaky on future runs until it is unmarked. Separately, under Flaky test options, clearing 'Flaky tests included in test pass percentage' removes both passed and failed results of flaky tests from the pass-percentage calculation (they instead appear under 'Tests not reported'), which prevents an intermittent failure in that test from failing the build. Disabling flaky test detection altogether would eliminate this management capability and cause every failure of the test to count as a real failure. Test Impact Analysis only limits which tests run based on code changes, and test slicing only partitions tests for parallel execution — neither affects how flaky failures are counted toward pipeline success or failure.

definition.explanation:
Azure Artifacts feeds support the concept of views (such as @Local, @Prerelease, and @Release), which let you promote a package through different stages within a single feed. By publishing all builds to the same feed but only exposing packages that have passed validation to a release view, you can control which package versions are visible to consumers, effectively restricting in-development packages from being released while still allowing multiple builds to share one feed. Upstream sources instead allow a feed to pull packages from other feeds or public registries and do not address restricting release visibility of packages within your own feed.

**Learn more:** [Views in Azure Artifacts feeds](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/artifacts/concepts/views)

By publishing all builds to the same feed but only exposing packages that have passed validation to a release view, you can control which package versions are visible to consumers, effectively restricting in-development packages from being released while still allowing multiple builds to share one feed. Upstream sources instead allow a feed to pull packages from other feeds or public registries and do not address restricting release visibility of packages within your own feed.

choices.label: B

definition.explanation:
Availability tests in Azure Application Insights allow you to configure synthetic tests (such as URL ping tests) that periodically send requests to your web app endpoint from multiple geographic locations and verify that it returns a successful HTTP status code (200) within an expected response time. When the test fails—such as when a non-200 status code is returned—Application Insights raises an availability alert, which can be configured with an action group to send an email notification to the DevOps team. Service Map and Application Map are used for visualizing application component dependencies and diagnosing performance/failure correlations, not for synthetic endpoint status monitoring, and Profiler is used for capturing detailed code-level performance traces of live requests, not availability checks.

**Learn more:** [Monitor the availability of any website - Azure Monitor | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/app/availability-overview)
