When the test fails—such as when a non-200 status code is returned—Application Insights raises an availability alert, which can be configured with an action group to send an email notification to the DevOps team. Service Map and Application Map are used for visualizing application component dependencies and diagnosing performance/failure correlations, not for synthetic endpoint status monitoring, and Profiler is used for capturing detailed code-level performance traces of live requests, not availability checks.

definition.stemRaw:
You have an existing build pipeline configured in Azure Pipelines.  
  
You need to enable incremental builds so that the environment is not purged between pipeline executions.  
  
What should you use?
definition.explanation:
A self-hosted agent is a machine you set up and maintain yourself to run pipeline jobs. Unlike Microsoft-hosted agents, which provision a fresh virtual machine for every job and discard it afterward, a self-hosted agent retains its working directories between runs by default (only the artifact staging directory and test results directory are cleaned). This persistence lets build tools reuse existing files and intermediate outputs, enabling incremental builds and deployments across pipeline executions without purging the environment each time.

**Learn more:** [Azure Pipelines Agents - Azure Pipelines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/agents/agents?view=azure-devops) · [Microsoft-hosted agents for Azure Pipelines - Azure Pipelines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/agents/hosted?view=azure-devops)

Unlike Microsoft-hosted agents, which provision a fresh virtual machine for every job and discard it afterward, a self-hosted agent retains its working directories between runs by default (only the artifact staging directory and test results directory are cleaned). You have an Azure DevOps organization named Contoso and an Azure subscription. The subscription includes an Azure virtual machine scale set named VMSS1 and an Azure Standard Load Balancer named LB1, where LB1 distributes incoming requests across the VMSS1 instances.  
  
You use Azure DevOps to build a web app named App1 and deploy it to VMSS1. App1 is accessible only over HTTPS and is configured to require mutual authentication using a client certificate.  
  
You need to recommend a solution for implementing a health check for App1 that meets the following requirements:  
  
- Identifies whether individual VMSS1 instances are eligible for an upgrade operation.  
- Minimizes administrative effort.  
  
What should you include in the recommendation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: an Azure Load Balancer health probe

finalExplanation: The Application Health extension runs on each virtual machine scale set instance and probes a specified application endpoint (using TCP, HTTP, or HTTPS), reporting the application's health status back to the Azure platform. Azure uses this health signal natively to determine whether an instance is healthy and eligible for upgrade operations (as well as for automatic instance repairs), without requiring custom scripting or manual health-check logic. In contrast, a Load Balancer health probe only informs load-balancing traffic decisions and is not designed to signal per-instance upgrade eligibility to the scale set's orchestration, Azure Monitor autoscale addresses scaling rather than upgrade health, and the Custom Script Extension would require building and maintaining custom health-check code, increasing administrative overhead.

definition.stemRaw:
You have a free-tier Azure DevOps organization named Contoso that contains 10 private projects. Each project has multiple jobs, and there are no dependencies between the jobs. The build process requires access to resource files that reside in an on-premises file system.  
  
You frequently run the jobs on five self-hosted agents, but you experience long build times and builds that are frequently queued.  
  
You need to minimize both the number of queued builds and the time it takes to run the builds.  
  
What should you do?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Configure the pipelines to use the Microsoft-hosted agents.

finalExplanation: Because the pipelines must access files on an on-premises file system, they must continue running on self-hosted agents rather than Microsoft-hosted agents. In Azure DevOps, the number of jobs that can execute simultaneously is governed by the number of parallel jobs (parallelism slots) an organization has, not by the number of agents registered in a pool. A free-tier organization is granted only one free self-hosted parallel job, so even with five agents available, only one job runs at a time while the rest queue. Adding more self-hosted agents would not change this limit, since the agents would still be constrained to the single available parallel job slot. Purchasing additional self-hosted parallel jobs increases the number of jobs that can run concurrently across the existing agent pool, directly reducing queuing and overall build time.

Neither agent alone provides this capability - the Dependency agent has no independent data channel and depends on the Log Analytics agent being installed on the same VM. definition.stemRaw:
Your team follows an agile development approach.  
  
You need to recommend a branching strategy for the team's Git repository. The strategy must meet the following requirements:  
  
- Provide the ability to work on multiple independent tasks in parallel.  
- Ensure that checked-in code remains in a releasable state at all times.  
- Ensure that new features can be abandoned at any time.  
- Encourage experimentation.  
  
What should you recommend?

choices.label: A
choices.text: a single long-running branch without forking

choices.label: C
choices.text: a single fork per team member

choices.label: D
choices.text: a single long-running branch with multiple short-lived feature branches

finalExplanation: A trunk-based approach that uses one long-running main branch together with multiple short-lived feature branches satisfies all of the stated requirements. Each task or feature is developed in its own short-lived branch, allowing several tasks to proceed in parallel without interfering with one another. Because the main branch only receives completed, reviewed, and tested work through merges, it remains in a releasable state at all times. Since each feature lives in its own isolated branch, that branch (and the feature) can be abandoned or deleted at any point without affecting the main branch or other in-progress work. The isolation also encourages experimentation, since developers can try out changes in a disposable branch without risk to the stable codebase. This is the branching model recommended in Microsoft's Azure Repos/Azure DevOps guidance for agile teams, as opposed to a single branch with no forking (no isolation), multiple long-running branches (integration and merge complexity, harder to keep releasable), or one fork per team member (oriented toward distributed/open-source contribution workflows rather than rapid, releasable agile delivery).

definition.stemRaw:
Your company builds a client banking application that handles a large volume of data. Code quality has been an ongoing concern, and it has recently worsened due to increased time pressure on the development team.  
  
You need to implement static code analysis.  
  
During which phase should you use static code analysis?
definition.explanation:
Static code analysis tools are designed to inspect source code automatically without executing it, and they are most effective when integrated directly into the build process (e.g., as a build step in a CI/CD pipeline). This ensures that every code change is analyzed for quality, style, and potential defects as soon as it is compiled, allowing issues to be caught and addressed immediately—before the code advances to integration testing, staging, or production release. Embedding static analysis in the build phase creates fast, continuous feedback for developers, which directly addresses code quality problems caused by time pressure, since issues are surfaced early rather than discovered later in the release pipeline.

**Learn more:** [Azure Pipelines - Configure code analysis](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/apps/aspnet/build-aspnet-4) · [SonarQube integration with Azure DevOps](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/ecosystems/sonarqube)

finalExplanation: Static code analysis tools are designed to inspect source code automatically without executing it, and they are most effective when integrated directly into the build process (e.g., as a build step in a CI/CD pipeline). This ensures that every code change is analyzed for quality, style, and potential defects as soon as it is compiled, allowing issues to be caught and addressed immediately—before the code advances to integration testing, staging, or production release. Embedding static analysis in the build phase creates fast, continuous feedback for developers, which directly addresses code quality problems caused by time pressure, since issues are surfaced early rather than discovered later in the release pipeline.

You have an on-premises Bitbucket Server with a firewall configured to block inbound Internet traffic. The server is used for Git-based source control.  
  
You intend to manage the build and release processes using Azure DevOps. This plan requires you to integrate Azure DevOps and Bitbucket.  
  
Which of the following will allow for this integration?

finalExplanation: Because the firewall blocks inbound Internet traffic to the on-premises Bitbucket Server, only outbound connections are possible from that network. A self-hosted build agent installed on-premises can reach the Bitbucket Server locally and communicates outbound to Azure Pipelines, so it does not require any inbound firewall exception; a Microsoft-hosted agent, running in Azure's cloud, would need inbound access to the on-premises server, which the firewall prevents. Since Azure Pipelines does not natively support Bitbucket Server (on-premises) as a repository type — native support exists only for Bitbucket Cloud — you must configure an External Git service connection to point to the on-premises Bitbucket Server URL. Service hooks are unrelated to this scenario, as they push notifications from Bitbucket Cloud to external services rather than enabling pipeline builds against an on-premises Git repository.

Solution: Create a main template that deploys the resources in one resource group and a nested template that deploys the resources in the other resource group.  
  
Does this meet the goal?
definition.explanation:
An ARM template can deploy to multiple resource groups by placing resources for the deployment’s target resource group in the main template and using a nested deployment targeted to the other resource group. The nested deployment specifies the destination resource group, allowing the virtual machines and SQL databases to be deployed to their respective groups.

**Learn more:** [Use Azure Resource Manager templates to deploy resources to resource groups](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/templates/deploy-to-resource-group)

The nested deployment specifies the destination resource group, allowing the virtual machines and SQL databases to be deployed to their respective groups.

definition.stemRaw:
Solution: Create a main template containing two linked templates, with each template deploying the resources in its corresponding group.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
definition.explanation:
A subscription-level ARM template can create the two resource groups and use linked deployments targeted at those resource groups. Linked templates support deploying resources to multiple resource groups in a single deployment, so separate linked templates can deploy the virtual machines and Azure SQL databases to their respective groups.

**Learn more:** [Use Azure Resource Manager templates to deploy resources to resource groups](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/templates/deploy-to-resource-group)

finalExplanation: A subscription-level ARM template can create the two resource groups and use linked deployments targeted at those resource groups. definition.stemRaw:
Solution: Create two standalone templates, each of which deploys the resources in its respective group.  
  
Does this meet the goal?
definition.explanation:
Resource-group-scoped ARM template deployments require the target resource group to exist. Creating resource groups requires a subscription-scope deployment; resources can then be deployed to those groups through nested or linked templates. Two standalone templates that only deploy resources into their respective groups do not create the two required resource groups.

**Learn more:** [Deploy resources to subscription - Azure Resource Manager](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/templates/deploy-to-subscription)

finalExplanation: Resource-group-scoped ARM template deployments require the target resource group to exist. Creating resource groups requires a subscription-scope deployment; resources can then be deployed to those groups through nested or linked templates. Two standalone templates that only deploy resources into their respective groups do not create the two required resource groups.

definition.stemRaw:
Solution: Create one standalone template to deploy all of the resources.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
definition.explanation:
Resources targeted at more than one resource group require deployments scoped to those groups, using nested or linked templates to target an additional resource group. A single standalone deployment template does not provide those separate resource-group scopes.

You must configure authentication for App1. The solution must accommodate the planned changes.  
  
Which three actions should be performed in sequence?

slots.answer: Configure the ID and secret for App1.

items: Configure the ID and secret for App1.

finalExplanation: Configuring an application to authenticate using an Azure AD app registration and client-secret credential (a classic service principal, as required when the planned changes explicitly call for App1 to use a service principal) follows three steps: register the application (creating an app registration, which automatically creates its backing service principal), add a client secret to that app registration, and then configure App1 itself with the application (client) ID and the generated secret so it can authenticate to Azure AD and obtain tokens. A managed identity does not use a manually configured ID/secret pair at all — Azure creates and rotates its credential automatically — so an approach built around 'configure the ID and secret for App1' is internally consistent only with an app-registration/service-principal secret, not a managed identity.

definition.stemRaw:
Your organization uses GitHub for source control. The GitHub repositories hold both source code and process documentation. The process documentation is authored as Microsoft Word documents that embed simple flow charts saved as .bmp files.  
  
You need to optimize how the process documentation and flow charts are integrated and versioned. The solution must meet these requirements:  
  
- Store documents as plain text.  
- Minimize the number of files that must be maintained.  
- Simplify the modification, merging, and reuse of flow charts.  
- Simplify the modification, merging, and reuse of documents.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1784178118801-6js37qkr.png)  
  
For each requirement in the answer area, select the appropriate conversion option.

finalExplanation: Markdown (.md) is a plain-text format that GitHub renders natively, making it simple to diff, merge, and reuse compared to binary Word .docx files, directly satisfying the 'store documents as plain text' and 'simplify modification, merging, and reuse of documents' requirements. Mermaid is a text-based diagramming syntax that GitHub renders inline within Markdown files (inside fenced code blocks with the mermaid language identifier). Because Mermaid diagrams are plain text, they can be embedded directly in the same Markdown file as the documentation, eliminating the need for separate .bmp image files (minimizing the number of files to maintain) and allowing the diagrams to be version-controlled, diffed, and merged just like any other text, which simplifies their modification, merging, and reuse.

definition.stemRaw: Which feature should be used to enforce the code quality restriction on the release pipeline for the investment planning applications suite?
definition.explanation:
Deployment gates in Azure Pipelines are automated checks configured as pre-deployment or post-deployment conditions on a release stage. They query external services or pipeline metrics—such as code coverage, pass rate, or other quality signals—and only allow the release to proceed to the next stage if those metrics meet a predefined threshold. This makes gates the appropriate mechanism for enforcing an objective, automated code quality restriction, as opposed to approvals (pre- or post-deployment), which require manual human sign-off, or triggers, which simply initiate pipeline execution based on events like commits or schedules.

**Learn more:** [Deployment gates concepts - Azure Pipelines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/approvals/gates?view=azure-devops)

This makes gates the appropriate mechanism for enforcing an objective, automated code quality restriction, as opposed to approvals (pre- or post-deployment), which require manual human sign-off, or triggers, which simply initiate pipeline execution based on events like commits or schedules.

definition.explanation:
Dependabot automatically scans a repository's dependency files, and when it finds an outdated or vulnerable dependency it creates a new branch with the required version change and opens a pull request for that change on its own — no manual branch creation or PR creation is needed. The engineer's first required action to move the update forward is to review and approve that automatically generated pull request, after which the associated Azure Pipelines build can validate the change and it can be merged/committed.

You plan to use Microsoft-hosted agents to build container images that will host full Microsoft .NET Framework apps in a YAML pipeline within Project1.  
  
Which two virtual machine images can you use for the Microsoft-hosted agent pool? Each correct answer presents a complete solution. (Choose two.)  
  
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
definition.explanation:
Microsoft-hosted agents offer a set of predefined VM images, each identified by an image name that you specify in the pool.vmImage property of a YAML pipeline. To build and host container images containing the full .NET Framework, a Windows-based image with the appropriate Windows Server/Windows 10 base and Docker tooling is required. Linux (ubuntu-16.04) and macOS (macOS-10.13) images cannot run or build full .NET Framework Windows containers, and 'vs.2015-win2012r2' is not offered/suitable for this container-build scenario.

**Learn more:** [Microsoft-hosted agents - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/agents/hosted)

finalExplanation: Microsoft-hosted agents offer a set of predefined VM images, each identified by an image name that you specify in the pool.vmImage property of a YAML pipeline. To build and host container images containing the full .NET Framework, a Windows-based image with the appropriate Windows Server/Windows 10 base and Docker tooling is required. The 'vs2017-win2016' image (Windows Server 2016 with Visual Studio 2017 and Docker support) and the 'win1803' image (Windows 10 version 1803) are both valid Microsoft-hosted images suited for building full .NET Framework container images. definition.stemRaw:
Your company has an Azure subscription named Subscription1, associated with an Azure Active Directory tenant named contoso.com.  
  
You need to provision an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster in Subscription1 and configure permissions for the cluster using RBAC roles that reference identities in contoso.com.  
  
Which three objects should you create, and in what sequence? Move the appropriate objects from the list to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.

finalExplanation: To integrate an AKS cluster with Azure Active Directory so that Kubernetes RBAC can reference AAD identities, you first register an application in the Azure AD tenant (contoso.com); this application (server/client app) is used by AKS for Azure AD authentication. You then provision the AKS cluster, enabling Azure AD integration and pointing it to the application registration created earlier. Finally, after the cluster is running, you create an RBAC role binding (or cluster role binding) in Kubernetes that maps the Azure AD user or group object to a Kubernetes Role or ClusterRole, granting the desired permissions. A system-assigned managed identity is unrelated to referencing AAD user/group identities for RBAC purposes and is not part of this required sequence.

definition.stemRaw: You are developing a Microsoft ASP.NET application that needs to support authentication. You need to authenticate users through Azure Active Directory (Azure AD). What should you do first?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Assign an enterprise application to users and groups

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an app registration in Azure AD

choices.label: C
choices.text: Configure the application to use a SAML endpoint

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a new OAuth token from the application

choices.label: E
choices.text: Create a membership database in an Azure SQL database

finalExplanation: Before an ASP.NET application can authenticate users against Azure AD, it must be registered in the Azure AD tenant via an app registration. This registration defines the application's identity (Application/client ID and tenant ID), configures redirect URIs, and sets up the permissions/scopes needed for the OpenID Connect/OAuth2 authentication flow that ASP.NET apps use with Azure AD. Without this registration, there is no application identity for Azure AD to issue tokens against, so subsequent steps such as configuring token acquisition or assigning users cannot occur. Microsoft's official tutorial for preparing a web application for Azure AD authentication begins with registering the application in the Microsoft identity platform (Azure AD) as the required first step.

definition.stemRaw:
You are automating the build process for a Java-based application using Azure DevOps.  
  
You need to add code coverage testing and publish the results to the pipeline.  
  
What should you use?

finalExplanation: Cobertura is a code coverage tool for Java applications that produces XML coverage reports (typically generated via Maven, Ant, or Gradle build plugins). Azure Pipelines' Publish Code Coverage Results task natively supports the Cobertura report format (along with JaCoCo) and uses it to generate an HTML code coverage report displayed under the Code Coverage tab of the pipeline run summary. The other options don't apply to Java: Bullseye Coverage is designed for C/C++ code, MSTest is a .NET testing framework, and Coverlet is a .NET-only cross-platform code coverage library — none of these can instrument or report coverage for Java code.

Your company has an Azure subscription. The company requires that all resource groups in the subscription have a tag named organization set to a value of Contoso. ![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783717181512-pzs3r7l6.png)
definition.explanation:
Azure Policy definitions use the 'type' field to scope the policy to a specific resource type; for resource groups the correct resource type value is 'Microsoft.Resources/subscriptions/resourceGroups'. 'Deny' would prevent creation of non-compliant resource groups instead of adding the tag, and 'DeployIfNotExists' is used for deploying related resources/templates, not for directly appending a tag value.

**Learn more:** [Azure Policy effects - Append](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/governance/policy/concepts/effects#append) · [Azure Policy definition structure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/governance/policy/concepts/definition-structure)

finalExplanation: Azure Policy definitions use the 'type' field to scope the policy to a specific resource type; for resource groups the correct resource type value is 'Microsoft.Resources/subscriptions/resourceGroups'. When the policy needs to automatically add a missing tag value rather than block the action, the 'Append' effect is used together with a 'details' array that specifies the field and value to apply. 'Deny' would prevent creation of non-compliant resource groups instead of adding the tag, and 'DeployIfNotExists' is used for deploying related resources/templates, not for directly appending a tag value.

definition.explanation:
Azure Pipelines variables can be scoped at the job, stage, pipeline root (top of YAML), and pipeline settings UI levels. When a variable with the same name exists at multiple scopes, the more locally scoped value takes precedence: job-level variables override stage-level variables, stage-level variables override pipeline root-level variables, and pipeline root-level variables override values set in the pipeline settings UI. Thus the precedence from highest to lowest is job, stage, pipeline root, pipeline settings UI, as described in Microsoft's documentation on defining variables in Azure Pipelines.

Which three commands should be run in sequence? Move the appropriate commands to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
definition.explanation:
Provisioning an RBAC-enabled AKS cluster with a custom (user-defined) service principal requires first creating that service principal with 'az ad sp create-for-rbac', which outputs the appId and password needed. Next, 'az aks create' is run with the --service-principal and --client-secret parameters (and RBAC enabled by default/--enable-rbac) to provision the cluster using that identity instead of a system-generated one. Finally, 'az aks get-credentials' downloads and merges the cluster credentials into the local kubeconfig so that kubectl and other tools can connect to the cluster.

**Learn more:** [Use a service principal with Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/aks/kubernetes-service-principal) · [az aks create](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cli/azure/aks#az-aks-create)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Configure RBAC for the key vault.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Modify the application to access the key vault.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Configure a Key Vault access policy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deploy an Azure Desired State Configuration (DSC) extension.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Deploy a virtual machine that uses a system-assigned managed identity.

finalExplanation: To let a VM retrieve secrets from Key Vault without embedding credentials, you deploy the VM with a system-assigned managed identity, which gives the VM an automatically managed Azure AD identity. You then configure a Key Vault access policy that grants that managed identity the appropriate permissions (e.g., get/list on secrets). Finally, the application itself must be modified to call the Key Vault endpoint/SDK using the managed identity's token to fetch the secret at runtime. RBAC is an alternate access-control mechanism for Key Vault and is not required when using access policies, and deploying a DSC extension does not address secret retrieval via managed identity.

definition.explanation:
Migrating TFS 2013 to Azure DevOps Services while preserving changeset and work item revision dates, migrating all artifacts, and minimizing effort requires using the Azure DevOps Data Migration Tool's Database Import Service, which imports a full TFS collection database and preserves original history/timestamps. Solution: Implement a pull request strategy that uses fast-forward merges.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
definition.explanation: A fast-forward merge preserves all commits from the source branch in the target branch and merely moves the target branch pointer forward. It therefore does not reduce the number of commits in the master branch; a squash merge is used when the pull request history must be condensed.

finalExplanation: A fast-forward merge preserves all commits from the source branch in the target branch and merely moves the target branch pointer forward. It therefore does not reduce the number of commits in the master branch; a squash merge is used when the pull request history must be condensed.

definition.stemRaw:
Solution: You implement a pull request strategy that uses squash merges.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
definition.explanation:
A squash merge condenses all commits from a pull request’s source branch into one new commit on the target branch. This produces a linear target-branch history with fewer commits, reducing the history volume in the master branch.

**Learn more:** [Merge strategies and squash merge - Azure Repos](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/repos/git/merging-with-squash?view=azure-devops)

finalExplanation: A squash merge condenses all commits from a pull request’s source branch into one new commit on the target branch. This produces a linear target-branch history with fewer commits, reducing the history volume in the master branch.

definition.stemRaw:
Solution: You implement a pull request strategy that uses an explicit merge.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
definition.explanation: An explicit merge preserves the individual commits from the pull request and adds a merge commit to the target branch history. This increases rather than reduces the master branch’s history volume; squash merging is the strategy that combines the pull request changes into a single commit.

finalExplanation: An explicit merge preserves the individual commits from the pull request and adds a merge commit to the target branch history. This increases rather than reduces the master branch’s history volume; squash merging is the strategy that combines the pull request changes into a single commit.

definition.stemRaw:
You need to run inline testing for an Azure DevOps pipeline that uses a Docker deployment model. Your solution must ensure that the test results are not published to the pipeline.  
  
What should you use to perform the inline testing?

finalExplanation: With Docker-based applications in Azure Pipelines, one documented approach is to build and test using a multi-stage Dockerfile: the build and test steps run inside the container as separate stages, and because the test outputs stay within the intermediate build stage(s), they are never copied out or published back to the Azure DevOps pipeline. This differs from approaches that use the Publish Test Results task (or copy test result files out of the container) to explicitly surface test results in the pipeline's Tests tab. A single-stage Dockerfile lacks this stage isolation, an AKS pod is a deployment/runtime construct rather than a build-time testing mechanism, and a Docker Compose file is used to orchestrate multiple containers rather than to isolate test execution within a build.

You are developing an ASP.NET Core application.  
  
You want to create an application utilization baseline by collecting telemetry data.  
  
You need to add code to the application so that it captures the telemetry data. The solution must minimize the cost of storing the telemetry data.  
  
Which two actions should you take? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.  
  
(Choose two.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add the <InitialSamplingPercentage>99</InitialSamplingPercentage> parameter to the ApplicationInsights.config file.

choices.label: B
choices.text: From the code of the application, enable adaptive sampling.

choices.label: C
choices.text: From the code of the application, add Azure Application Insights telemetry.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add the <MaxTelemetryItemsPerSecond>5</MaxTelemetryItemsPerSecond> parameter to the ApplicationInsights.config file.

choices.label: E
choices.text: From the code of the application, disable adaptive sampling.

definition.explanation:
Capturing telemetry for a usage baseline requires instrumenting the application with Azure Application Insights telemetry collection in code. To keep storage costs low while still gathering representative data, Application Insights' adaptive sampling should be enabled (it is the SDK's default behavior), as it dynamically reduces the volume of telemetry sent to the service based on traffic while maintaining accurate aggregated metrics, thereby minimizing data ingestion and storage costs. Manually setting fixed sampling percentages or item-per-second limits in the config file, or disabling adaptive sampling, does not achieve the same cost-effective, self-adjusting reduction in telemetry volume.

**Learn more:** [Sampling in Application Insights](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/app/sampling)

finalExplanation: Capturing telemetry for a usage baseline requires instrumenting the application with Azure Application Insights telemetry collection in code. To keep storage costs low while still gathering representative data, Application Insights' adaptive sampling should be enabled (it is the SDK's default behavior), as it dynamically reduces the volume of telemetry sent to the service based on traffic while maintaining accurate aggregated metrics, thereby minimizing data ingestion and storage costs. Manually setting fixed sampling percentages or item-per-second limits in the config file, or disabling adaptive sampling, does not achieve the same cost-effective, self-adjusting reduction in telemetry volume.

Branch security controls user/group permissions on the branch but does not enforce PR workflows or approval gates, and the Services and Deployment pools settings in Project Settings relate to service connections and build/release agent pools, not branch protection or code review enforcement.

finalExplanation:
The rolling deployment strategy replaces instances of the previous version of an application with instances of the new version on a fixed set of machines (the rolling set) in each iteration, which matches App1's requirement to replace a fixed set of existing VM instances with the new version in each iteration while minimizing downtime.


The canary deployment strategy rolls out changes to a small subset of servers or pods first to validate functionality, then expands the rollout once validation succeeds — matching App2's requirement of a limited AKS deployment that expands after successful testing.


The runOnce strategy deploys all lifecycle hooks a single time to all targets at once, which does not support either the fixed-set iterative replacement (App1) or the limited/expanding validation rollout (App2), and would not minimize downtime as effectively.

You need to:  

- Run a URL ping test once every five minutes.  
- Create an alert that triggers when the web app is unavailable, as detected from specific Azure regions.

What should you do?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create an Azure Monitor Availability metric and alert.

choices.label: B

finalExplanation: Azure Application Insights availability tests (URL ping/standard tests) natively support running a ping test on a configurable interval, including every 5 minutes, and let you select specific Azure regions (test locations) from which the test is executed. An associated alert rule can then be configured to fire based on failures detected from those chosen locations, all through portal/ARM configuration without writing custom monitoring code, which satisfies the requirement to minimize development time. Deploying a custom Azure Function to multiple regions (option C) would require significant custom development. Azure Service Health (option D) reports on Azure platform incidents and planned maintenance, not application-level endpoint availability. There is no separate "Azure Monitor Availability metric" feature (option A) distinct from Application Insights availability tests that provides per-region ping testing and alerting.

definition.stemRaw:
App1 is an application that manages events across multiple locations and writes logs to a Log Analytics workspace named Workspace1, which contains two tables: Events and Logs.

definition.explanation:

statements.text: Job E can start before job C completes.

definition.stemRaw:
You have an Azure subscription containing a resource group named RG1. RG1 includes the following resources:  
  
- Four Azure virtual machines running Windows Server with Internet Information Services (IIS) installed  
- SQL Server on an Azure virtual machine  
- An Azure Load Balancer  
  
You need to deploy an application to the virtual machines in RG1 by using Azure Pipelines.  
  
Which four actions should you perform, in sequence? Move the appropriate actions to the answer area and arrange them in order.  
  
Note: More than one order of answer choices is correct. You will receive credit for any of the correct orders you select.

slots.label: Step 2
slots.answer: Add the Azure Pipelines Agent extension to the virtual machines

slots.label: Step 3
slots.answer: Add and configure a deployment group job for the pipeline

items: Add the Puppet Agent extension to the virtual machines
Add and configure a deployment group job for the pipeline
Add the Azure Pipelines Agent extension to the virtual machines

finalExplanation: Deploying to multiple Azure VMs using Azure Pipelines is accomplished with Deployment Groups. First, you create a deployment group in Azure DevOps (Pipelines > Deployment groups), which provides a registration script and target definition. Next, you add the Azure Pipelines Agent extension to each virtual machine (either by running the generated registration script on each VM or by adding the extension directly through the Azure VM's Extensions blade), which installs and registers the agent with the deployment group so the VM becomes a deployment target. Then, in the release/pipeline definition, you add and configure a deployment group job, specifying the deployment group as the target so the pipeline's tasks run against all registered VMs. Finally, you execute (queue) the pipeline to perform the actual application deployment across the VMs. Creating an agent pool is unrelated to deployment groups (agent pools serve build/release hosted agents), and the Puppet Agent extension is not part of Azure Pipelines deployment tooling.

You have a project in Azure DevOps named Project1 that contains two Azure DevOps pipelines named Pipeline1 and Pipeline2.  
  
You need to ensure that Pipeline1 can deploy code successfully to an Azure web app named webapp1. The solution must also ensure that Pipeline2 does not have permission to webapp1.  
  
Which three actions should you perform in sequence?

slots.answer: Create a service principal in Azure Active Directory.
In Project1, create a service connection.
In Pipeline1, authorize the service connection.

items: Create a service principal in Azure Active Directory.
In Project1, create a service connection.
In Pipeline1, authorize the service connection.
Create a system-assigned managed identity in Azure Active Directory.

finalExplanation: Azure DevOps service connections authenticate to Azure resources using credentials such as a service principal. To let Pipeline1 deploy to webapp1 while explicitly denying Pipeline2 access, you first create a service principal in Azure AD that has the required permissions on the web app. Next, in Project1 you create a service connection (Azure Resource Manager) that uses this service principal — if you do not enable 'Grant access permission to all pipelines' during creation, the connection is restricted and no pipeline can use it by default. Finally, in Pipeline1 you explicitly authorize that service connection, which grants only Pipeline1 permission to use it for deployment. Because Pipeline2 is never authorized against this service connection, it has no access to webapp1, satisfying both requirements.

definition.stemRaw:
You use GitHub to host container packages that use Semantic Versioning (SemVer).  
  
You have an app named App1. The current version of App1 is 11.2.0.  
  
You change the code of App1 to fix a bug that was introduced in version 10.5.1.  
  
Which version number should you assign to the release?
definition.explanation: Following semantic versioning, when the current production version is 11.2.0 and you're releasing a bug fix (regardless of which older version introduced the bug), you increment only the patch number (the third digit). Thus the version becomes 11.2.1. The original version in which the bug was introduced does not affect the versioning of the current release.

definition.stemRaw: Your company is building a new web application. You plan to collect feedback from pilot users on the features being delivered. All pilot users have a corporate computer with Google Chrome and the Microsoft Test & Feedback extension installed, and they will test the application using Chrome. You need to identify the access levels required so that developers can request and gather feedback from the pilot users, applying the principle of least privilege. Which access levels in Azure DevOps should you identify?
definition.explanation:
Requesting feedback in Azure DevOps (creating and sending a formal Feedback Request work item) requires at least Basic access, since Stakeholder access does not include the ability to request feedback. Developers who need to send feedback requests to pilot users must therefore be granted Basic access. Pilot users, on the other hand, only need to respond to feedback requests using the Test & Feedback browser extension (capturing screenshots, notes, and creating bugs/tasks), which is fully supported by the free Stakeholder access level. Assigning Stakeholder access to pilot users satisfies the principle of least privilege while still allowing them to provide feedback.

**Learn more:** [Request and provide stakeholder feedback - Azure Test Plans](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/test/request-stakeholder-feedback?view=azure-devops) · [About access levels - Azure DevOps](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/organizations/security/access-levels?view=azure-devops)

Developers who need to send feedback requests to pilot users must therefore be granted Basic access. Pilot users, on the other hand, only need to respond to feedback requests using the Test & Feedback browser extension (capturing screenshots, notes, and creating bugs/tasks), which is fully supported by the free Stakeholder access level. Assigning Stakeholder access to pilot users satisfies the principle of least privilege while still allowing them to provide feedback.

definition.explanation:
Azure Artifacts feed permission levels grant cumulative capabilities: Reader can only list/download/install packages; Collaborator adds the ability to save packages from an upstream source; Contributor (Feed Publisher) adds the ability to publish, promote, and deprecate packages; Owner adds full administrative control, including editing feed settings, managing upstream sources, and changing feed permissions, in addition to all Contributor capabilities. Because the Developers group only needs to install packages, Reader is the least-privileged sufficient role. Because the Team Leaders group must both publish new packages and edit feed permissions—and only the Owner role can modify feed permissions/settings—Team Leaders must be granted Owner access.

Because the Developers group only needs to install packages, Reader is the least-privileged sufficient role. Because the Team Leaders group must both publish new packages and edit feed permissions—and only the Owner role can modify feed permissions/settings—Team Leaders must be granted Owner access.

definition.stemRaw:
Your company develops an application named App1 that is deployed in production.  
  
As part of an update to App1, a new service is being added. This new service requires access to an application named App2, which is currently still in development.  
  
You need to ensure that you can deploy the App1 update before App2 becomes available, while also being able to enable the new service in App1 once App2 has been deployed.  
  
What should you do?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a fork in the build.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a branch in the build.

definition.explanation:
A feature flag (feature toggle) lets you deploy code for a new capability while keeping it disabled in production. This decouples deployment from release: App1 can be updated and shipped immediately, and once the dependent App2 becomes available, the flag can simply be turned on to enable the new service—without requiring a new deployment. Forking, branching, and branch policies are source-control/build practices for managing code changes and enforcing quality gates during development; they do not provide a mechanism to control whether a feature is active in a running production application.

**Learn more:** [Feature flags in Azure DevOps / feature management overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-app-configuration/concept-feature-management)

finalExplanation: A feature flag (feature toggle) lets you deploy code for a new capability while keeping it disabled in production. This decouples deployment from release: App1 can be updated and shipped immediately, and once the dependent App2 becomes available, the flag can simply be turned on to enable the new service—without requiring a new deployment. Forking, branching, and branch policies are source-control/build practices for managing code changes and enforcing quality gates during development; they do not provide a mechanism to control whether a feature is active in a running production application.

This is the built-in Azure capability designed to evaluate and recommend security improvements for these compute resources, unlike Log Analytics' Security & Compliance solution, Service Health's Resource Health (which tracks availability, not security), or Application Insights Smart Detection (which flags performance/failure anomalies rather than security configuration issues).

You have a GitHub organization named org1 and an Azure tenant named Tenant1.  
  
You need to enable single sign-on (SSO) in Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) for the users in org1.  
  
Which URIs should you use for the SAML configuration in Azure AD? Each URI may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

finalExplanation: When configuring a GitHub Enterprise Cloud organization for SAML single sign-on with Azure AD (Microsoft Entra ID), the Basic SAML Configuration section requires three organization-specific URLs on the GitHub side: the Identifier (Entity ID) is https://github.com/orgs/<organization>, which uniquely identifies the GitHub organization as the SAML service provider; the Reply URL (Assertion Consumer Service URL) is https://github.com/orgs/<organization>/saml/consume, the endpoint where Azure AD posts the SAML assertion after successful authentication; and the Sign on URL is https://github.com/orgs/<organization>/sso, the URL users are redirected to for organization-based sign-on. Substituting org1 for <organization> gives the correct values for each field. The login.microsoftonline.com URLs are Azure AD-side endpoints and are not used in these GitHub SP configuration fields.

finalExplanation: Azure Application Insights is an Application Performance Management (APM) service that collects telemetry from web applications, including client-side browser telemetry such as page load times, AJAX call durations, and server response times. definition.stemRaw: You are finalizing a release in GitHub. You need to apply the following labels to the release: Name, Email, Release v3.0, and Release date. How should you complete the git command?
definition.explanation:
Creating an annotated tag with 'git tag -a <tagname> -m "<message>"' stores a full tag object in the Git database that includes the tagger's name, the tagger's email address, the date the tag was created, and the tag message. A lightweight tag (created with plain 'git tag <tagname>') stores none of this metadata - it is just a reference to a commit. Since the release requires Name, Email, Release date, and the 'Release v3.0' message to be recorded, the annotated tag option '-a' must be used together with '-m' to supply the message text. The resulting command is 'git tag -a v3.0 -m "Release v3.0"'.

**Learn more:** [Git - Tagging](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Basics-Tagging)

finalExplanation: Creating an annotated tag with 'git tag -a <tagname> -m "<message>"' stores a full tag object in the Git database that includes the tagger's name, the tagger's email address, the date the tag was created, and the tag message. A lightweight tag (created with plain 'git tag <tagname>') stores none of this metadata - it is just a reference to a commit. Since the release requires Name, Email, Release date, and the 'Release v3.0' message to be recorded, the annotated tag option '-a' must be used together with '-m' to supply the message text. The resulting command is 'git tag -a v3.0 -m "Release v3.0"'.

Your organization has a team of 500 developers, and new members are continually being added to this team.  
  
You need to automate the management of users and licenses wherever possible.  
  
Which of the following tasks must you still perform manually?
definition.explanation:
Azure DevOps can automate adding users, assigning entitlements, and updating group memberships by using Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) group rules, which automatically grant access levels and entitlements to users based on their group membership when they first sign in. However, procuring the licenses themselves — determining how many and which type of licenses to purchase and completing that purchase — is a commercial/administrative decision that Azure DevOps cannot automate; an administrator must manually acquire the licenses before they can be assigned through group rules.

definition.stemRaw:
You have an Azure DevOps organization named Contoso and an Azure subscription.  
  
You use Azure DevOps to build a containerized app named App1 and deploy App1 to an Azure container instance named ACI1.  
  
You need to configure ACI1 so that it restarts automatically when App1 stops responding.  
  
What should you do?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a liveness probe to the YAML configuration of App1.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add a readiness probe to the YAML configuration of App1.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use Connection Monitor in Azure Network Watcher.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use IP flow verify in Azure Network Watcher.

finalExplanation: A liveness probe periodically checks whether the application running in a container instance is still functioning correctly. If the probe fails (for example, because the app stops responding), Azure Container Instances kills the container and restarts it, according to the group's restart policy. A readiness probe only determines whether the container is ready to receive traffic and does not cause a restart on failure. Network Watcher's Connection Monitor and IP flow verify are network diagnostic tools used to test connectivity and security rules, not to monitor application health or trigger container restarts. Configuring a livenessProbe section in the ACI YAML deployment is therefore the correct mechanism to restart ACI1 when App1 becomes unresponsive.

definition.stemRaw: You have a GitHub repository containing the code for an app named App1. App1 depends on a library of functions from a repository located at https://github.com/contoso/afeed. definition.explanation:
Git submodules let you keep a clone of one Git repository as a subdirectory inside another Git repository, while tracking that subdirectory at a specific commit and keeping its history separate from the parent repository. The command 'git submodule add <repository-url>' clones the specified repository into a subdirectory of the current repository and registers it in a .gitmodules file, which is exactly the behavior required to embed the afeed repository inside the App1 repository. A plain 'git clone' would only create an independent copy of afeed and would not link it as a tracked component of App1's repository.

definition.stemRaw: How should you configure the release retention policy for the investment planning depletions suite?

finalExplanation: Extending release retention beyond the built-in Azure DevOps retention window typically requires a script or pipeline task that copies the release artifacts to external Azure Blob Storage before they are purged. Authorizing that script's requests against the storage account requires a Shared Access Signature (a 'Shared Access Authorization token'), since it grants time-limited, scoped access without exposing the storage account key, unlike a personal access token (which authenticates against Azure DevOps, not Azure Storage) or a certificate/username-password pair. Microsoft Azure Storage best practices explicitly require that SAS tokens be created and transmitted only over HTTPS, because a SAS sent over plain HTTP can be intercepted and reused by an attacker to access the storage account. Azure Data Lake and Azure Key Vault are not appropriate here because Data Lake is intended for big-data analytics storage and Key Vault is intended for storing secrets/keys/certificates, not archived release artifacts.

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.text: ensures that all traffic to new Azure Storage accounts is encrypted

choices.label: C
choices.text: prevents HTTPS traffic to new Azure Storage accounts when the accounts are accessed over the Internet

choices.label: D
choices.text: ensures that all data for new Azure Storage accounts is encrypted at rest

finalExplanation: The policy's condition checks whether a resource is of type Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts and whether its supportsHttpsTrafficOnly property is not equal to true; when both conditions are met, the effect is deny. Because deny is evaluated during resource creation or update in Resource Manager mode, it blocks the creation (or modification) of any storage account that doesn't have supportsHttpsTrafficOnly set to true, effectively requiring all new storage accounts to enforce HTTPS-only (encrypted) traffic. It does not affect traffic to already-existing storage accounts (those are only flagged as non-compliant), and supportsHttpsTrafficOnly governs encryption of data in transit, not encryption at rest.

You have an Azure DevOps pipeline used to deploy a Node.js application. You need to make sure the dependencies are cached between builds. How should you configure the deployment YAML? Drag the appropriate values to the correct targets in the pipeline definition. Each value may be used once, more than once, or not at all.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1784186900511-aiyxlwr4.png)
definition.template:
…
variables:
  npm_config_cache: $(Pipeline.Workspace)/.npm

steps:
- task: Cache@2
  inputs:
    key: 'npm | "$(Agent.OS)" | package-lock.json'
    restoreKeys: |
       npm | "$(Agent.OS)"
    path: $(npm_config_cache)
    cacheHitVar: CACHE_RESTORED

- script: {{script}}
  condition: {{condition}}
…
definition.explanation:
The Cache@2 task's cacheHitVar output variable (CACHE_RESTORED) indicates whether the npm cache was successfully restored. To ensure dependencies are cached between builds while still installing them when needed, the pipeline should run 'npm install' only when the cache was not restored, using condition: ne(variables.CACHE_RESTORED, 'true'). This pattern skips the install step on a cache hit (saving build time) and runs it on a cache miss (ensuring dependencies exist), which satisfies the requirement to cache dependencies between builds.

**Learn more:** [Pipeline caching - Azure Pipelines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/caching?view=azure-devops) · [Cache@2 - Cache v2 task | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/tasks/reference/cache-v2?view=azure-pipelines)

To ensure dependencies are cached between builds while still installing them when needed, the pipeline should run 'npm install' only when the cache was not restored, using condition: ne(variables.CACHE_RESTORED, 'true'). This pattern skips the install step on a cache hit (saving build time) and runs it on a cache miss (ensuring dependencies exist), which satisfies the requirement to cache dependencies between builds.

...

requests
| where {{time_filter}}
| where resultCode == “404” and (client_City == “London” or client_City == “Paris”)

You use Git for source control and need to optimize a repository's performance. The solution must meet these requirements:  
  
- Permanently remove all items referenced only in the reflog.  
- Remove history that is not part of any current branch.  
  
How should you complete the commands?
definition.template:
git {{cmd1}} expire --expire-unreachable=now --all
git {{cmd2}} --prune={{prune}}
definition.explanation:
'git reflog expire --expire-unreachable=now --all' immediately expires (deletes) reflog entries that point to unreachable commits across all refs, which permanently removes items that are referenced only in the reflog. 'git gc --prune=now' runs garbage collection and immediately prunes all objects that are no longer reachable from any branch or tag (bypassing the default 2-week grace period used by --prune=<date>), which removes history that is not part of any current branch. Using --prune=now ensures unreachable commits, including those just expired from the reflog, are removed right away rather than being retained temporarily.

**Learn more:** [git-reflog Documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-reflog) · [git-gc Documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-gc)

finalExplanation: 'git reflog expire --expire-unreachable=now --all' immediately expires (deletes) reflog entries that point to unreachable commits across all refs, which permanently removes items that are referenced only in the reflog. 'git gc --prune=now' runs garbage collection and immediately prunes all objects that are no longer reachable from any branch or tag (bypassing the default 2-week grace period used by --prune=<date>), which removes history that is not part of any current branch. finalExplanation: The Local Configuration Manager (LCM) runs on every DSC target node and its ConfigurationMode property determines how the node applies and maintains its desired state configuration. The available values are ApplyOnly (apply once, no ongoing drift correction), ApplyAndMonitor (apply and log drift only, the default), and ApplyAndAutoCorrect (apply, detect drift, and automatically reapply the configuration to correct it). Since the VMs in Pool7 have already been registered as managed nodes, the remaining step needed to ensure the servers continue to comply with their assigned configuration—correcting any drift that occurs after initial deployment—is to modify the ConfigurationMode property of the LCM (typically setting it to ApplyAndAutoCorrect). This setting change currently requires re-registering the node, as DSC LCM values set during initial registration can only be altered through re-registration.

Which two approaches can be used to integrate ServiceNow into the Azure DevOps release pipeline? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.  
  
(Choose two. Each correct selection is worth one point.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Define a deployment control that invokes the ServiceNow REST API.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Define a pre-deployment gate before the deployment to the Prod stage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Define a deployment control that invokes the ServiceNow SOAP API.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Define a post-deployment gate after the deployment to the QA stage.

finalExplanation: The official ServiceNow Change Management extension for Azure Pipelines provides two integration mechanisms: a pre-deployment gate that blocks progression to a stage (such as Prod) until the linked ServiceNow change request satisfies the configured condition, and an agentless deployment task/control that calls the ServiceNow REST API to create, query, or update a change request during the release. Using either mechanism on the Prod stage's pre-deployment conditions ensures deployment cannot proceed until the change request has been processed. The integration communicates with ServiceNow over its REST API (not SOAP), and the control must be applied before the Prod deployment, not after a QA deployment, to actually gate the production release.

Your organization uses Azure DevOps to manage build and release processes for its applications, with source control handled through a Git repository.  
  
You are planning to create a new branch based on an existing pull request. Afterward, you intend to merge this new branch into the pull request's target branch.  
  
You need to select a pull request action to create the new branch, ensuring that the branch includes only part of the code contained in the pull request.  
  
Which pull request action should you use?
definition.explanation:
The Cherry-pick pull request action in Azure DevOps allows you to take a specific commit (or a subset of commits) from a pull request and apply it to a new branch, rather than including all the changes from the entire pull request. This lets you create a branch containing only a portion of the PR's code, which can then be merged into the target branch later. Other actions like Revert apply to the whole PR's changes, Reactivate reopens an abandoned PR, and Approve with suggestions is merely a review vote option — none of these create a branch with a partial set of the PR's changes.

**Learn more:** [Cherry-pick or revert changes with pull requests - Azure Repos](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/repos/git/cherry-pick?view=azure-devops)

definition.stemRaw: You have an Azure web app named Webapp1. You need to write an Azure Monitor query to generate a report showing the top 10 pages of Webapp1 that failed. How should you complete the query?

finalExplanation: HTTP request telemetry for a web app, including whether each request succeeded or failed, is stored in the Application Insights 'requests' table. The 'exceptions' table stores exception telemetry, 'pageViews' stores client-side page view events (no failure status), and 'traces' stores custom log/diagnostic messages — none of these track request success/failure by HTTP result code. The boolean field 'success' is automatically populated by the Application Insights SDK based on the HTTP status code returned (4xx/5xx are marked as failed), so filtering with 'success == false' correctly isolates failed requests. The other candidate filters are unrelated: 'duration == 0' checks request duration, 'itemType == "availabilityResult"' pertains to availability test results, and 'resultCode == "200"' actually identifies successful (not failed) requests. This matches Microsoft's documented example query for 'Failed requests – top 10' against the requests/AppRequests table.

items: Add an Azure Resource Group Deployment task.

finalExplanation: To deploy resources to Azure from an ARM template hosted on GitHub as part of a CI/CD process, you first create a release pipeline in Azure Pipelines that connects to the GitHub repository as its artifact source. definition.stemRaw: You have a build pipeline configured in Azure Pipelines. You create a Slack App Integration. You need to send build notifications to a Slack channel named #Development. What should you do first?

definition.stemRaw:
You plan to share packages that you have written, tested, validated, and deployed by using Azure Artifacts.  
  
You need to release multiple builds of each package through a single feed. The solution must limit the release of packages that are still in development.  
  
What should you use?
definition.explanation:
Azure Artifacts feeds allow multiple package versions to exist under one feed, and each feed automatically includes three views: @Local, @Prerelease, and @Release. By promoting packages through these views as they pass testing and validation, you can restrict consumers to only the @Release view, ensuring that in-development or unvalidated builds (which remain in @Local) are not exposed. This lets a single feed host multiple builds of a package while controlling which ones are released to consumers.

**Learn more:** [What are feed views? - Azure Artifacts | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/artifacts/concepts/views?view=azure-devops) · [Promote packages and manage feed views - Azure Artifacts | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/artifacts/feeds/views?view=azure-devops)

By promoting packages through these views as they pass testing and validation, you can restrict consumers to only the @Release view, ensuring that in-development or unvalidated builds (which remain in @Local) are not exposed. This lets a single feed host multiple builds of a package while controlling which ones are released to consumers.

definition.stemRaw:
Your company uses Git as a source control system for a complex application named App1.  
  
You are planning to add new functionality to App1 and need to design a branching model for this new feature.  
  
Which branch lifetime and branch type should be used in the branching model?
definition.explanation:
When adding new functionality to an application, the recommended Git branching practice is to create a dedicated feature branch off of the main/develop branch. Feature branches are short-lived by design: they are created specifically to develop one piece of functionality, used only for the duration of that work, and then merged into the main line and deleted once the feature is complete. This contrasts with long-lived branches such as master/main or integration branches (e.g., develop), which persist for the entire lifetime of the project. Therefore, for new functionality the correct branch type is 'Feature' and the correct branch lifetime is 'Short-lived'.

**Learn more:** [Git - Branching Workflows](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Branching-Branching-Workflows) · [A successful Git branching model » nvie.com](https://nvie.com/posts/a-successful-git-branching-model/)

Feature branches are short-lived by design: they are created specifically to develop one piece of functionality, used only for the duration of that work, and then merged into the main line and deleted once the feature is complete. This contrasts with long-lived branches such as master/main or integration branches (e.g., develop), which persist for the entire lifetime of the project. Therefore, for new functionality the correct branch type is 'Feature' and the correct branch lifetime is 'Short-lived'.

definition.stemRaw:
You use Azure Pipelines pipeline to build and deploy an app named App1.  
  
You need to ensure that before App1 is deployed, all the code for the app passes a security validation by using a custom tool.  
  
What should you do?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add a status check to the policies of the main branch.

choices.text: Add a service hook to the project.

definition.explanation:
Since App1 is deployed from code that lands on the main branch, requiring the custom security tool as a status check in the main branch's policies guarantees no pull request can complete, and therefore no code can reach the deployment stage, until the tool reports success. Gating only the branch used by the development department would leave other paths into main (such as hotfixes or merges from other teams) unchecked, so deployed code would not be reliably validated.

You have a project in Azure DevOps named Project1. Project1 contains a build pipeline named Pipe1 that builds an application named App1.  
  
You have an agent pool named Pool1 that contains a Windows Server 2019-based self-hosted agent. Pipe1 uses Pool1.  
  
You are planning to implement another project named Project2. Project2 will have a build pipeline named Pipe2 that builds an application named App2.  
  
App1 and App2 have conflicting dependencies.  
  
You need to minimize the possibility that the two build pipelines will conflict with each other. The solution must also minimize infrastructure costs.  
  
What should you do?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add a Docker Compose task to the build pipelines.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the self-hosted agent to use Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 8.

definition.explanation:
Azure Pipelines allows a job to run inside a Docker container on a self-hosted agent by defining a container job. This isolates each pipeline's build tools and dependencies within their own container, so App1's and App2's conflicting dependencies never interact, even though both pipelines still use the same underlying self-hosted agent in Pool1. This avoids the cost of provisioning and maintaining additional agent infrastructure (unlike adding another self-hosted agent), and directly resolves the dependency isolation problem, which a Docker Compose task (intended for multi-container image build/push orchestration) or an OS change to the agent would not address.

**Learn more:** [Container jobs - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/process/container-phases)

This avoids the cost of provisioning and maintaining additional agent infrastructure (unlike adding another self-hosted agent), and directly resolves the dependency isolation problem, which a Docker Compose task (intended for multi-container image build/push orchestration) or an OS change to the agent would not address.

Which role should you assign to User1?
definition.explanation: The Deployment Environments User role is the minimal role required to provision environments in Azure Deployment Environments. Which version control solution should you choose?
definition.explanation:
Git is a distributed version control system, meaning every developer's local repository contains a full copy of the project's history. This enables developers to commit changes, create branches, and browse the entire history offline, then synchronize with the shared remote repository once connectivity is restored. In contrast, Team Foundation Version Control (TFVC) is a centralized system that generally requires a connection to the server for history and most source control operations, making it unsuitable for frequent offline work with full history access.

A deployment group is a logical set of target machines, each running a deployment agent, that communicate with Azure Pipelines to coordinate application deployment. Deployment groups work identically for machines hosted in Azure and machines hosted on-premises — the only requirement is that the Azure Pipelines (deployment group) agent is installed and registered on each target, which is already true for all 20 machines in this scenario. items: Save the SSH key to the root of repo1.

definition.explanation:
To authenticate to an Azure Repos Git repository using SSH, you must first sign in to Azure DevOps, then generate an SSH key pair locally using the ssh-keygen utility. Next, you add the generated public key to your Azure DevOps user profile (under SSH public keys), which allows Azure DevOps to verify your identity when you connect over SSH. Finally, you clone the repository using its SSH clone URL, at which point Git uses the local private key (paired with the public key registered in Azure DevOps) to authenticate. The private key is never uploaded to Azure DevOps or stored in the repository — it remains only on the client machine, so 'Add the SSH private key' and 'Save the SSH key to the root of repo1' are not valid steps.

**Learn more:** [Use SSH key authentication - Azure Repos | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/repos/git/use-ssh-keys-to-authenticate?view=azure-devops)

Finally, you clone the repository using its SSH clone URL, at which point Git uses the local private key (paired with the public key registered in Azure DevOps) to authenticate. definition.stemRaw:
You have an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) pod. You need to configure a probe that:  
  
- Confirms the pod is responding to service requests  
- Checks the status of the pod four times a minute  
- Initiates a shutdown if the pod is unresponsive  
  
How should you complete the YAML configuration file shown below?
definition.template:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
    labels:
        test: readiness-and-liveness
    name: readiness-http
spec:
    containers:
    - name: container1
      image: k8s.gcr.io/readiness-and-liveness
      args:
      - /server
      {{probeType}}
          httpGet:
              path: /checknow
              port: 8123
              httpHeaders:
              - name: Custom-Header
                value: CheckNow
              {{period}}
definition.explanation:
A livenessProbe is the Kubernetes probe type used to determine whether a container should be restarted (i.e., have Kubernetes initiate a shutdown/restart of the pod) when it stops responding to requests; readinessProbe only controls whether the pod receives traffic and does not restart it, and 'ShutdownProbe' does not exist as a Kubernetes probe kind. The periodSeconds field controls how often (in seconds) the kubelet performs the probe; to check the pod's status four times per minute you need an interval of 60/4 = 15 seconds, i.e., periodSeconds: 15.

**Learn more:** [Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes - Kubernetes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/) · [Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes - Kubernetes Concepts](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/probes/)

finalExplanation: A livenessProbe is the Kubernetes probe type used to determine whether a container should be restarted (i.e., have Kubernetes initiate a shutdown/restart of the pod) when it stops responding to requests; readinessProbe only controls whether the pod receives traffic and does not restart it, and 'ShutdownProbe' does not exist as a Kubernetes probe kind. The periodSeconds field controls how often (in seconds) the kubelet performs the probe; to check the pod's status four times per minute you need an interval of 60/4 = 15 seconds, i.e., periodSeconds: 15.

You need to set up GitHub so that it uses Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) for authentication.  
  
What should you do first?

choices.label: A

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create an Azure Active Directory B2C (Azure AD B2C) tenant.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Modify the Security settings of the GitHub organization.

definition.explanation:
To integrate GitHub Enterprise Cloud with Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) for single sign-on, the first step is to add GitHub from the Azure AD application gallery as an enterprise application (registering GitHub in Azure AD). This registration generates the SAML configuration values (Entra Identifier, Login URL, and signing certificate) that are required later when enabling SAML authentication in the GitHub organization's Security settings. Only after GitHub is registered as an application in Azure AD can the SAML configuration be completed on both the Azure AD side and the GitHub side.

blanks.label: How many stages have triggers set?
Which component should you modify to enable continuous delivery?

definition.explanation:
Classic release pipelines configure a deployment trigger for each stage through pre-deployment conditions. A trigger can be After release, After stage, or Manual only; therefore all seven stages have a trigger configuration. Continuous delivery requires the deployment path to proceed automatically: with the artifact trigger already enabled, the Internal Review stage’s manual-only trigger is the remaining interruption and must be changed to an automatic stage trigger. Microsoft documents that continuous deployment is enabled from the artifact’s trigger settings and that stage triggers are configured in each stage’s pre-deployment conditions.

**Learn more:** [Classic release triggers - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/ga-ie/azure/devops/pipelines/release/triggers?view=azure-devops-server) · [Create a multi-stage Classic release pipeline - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/define-multistage-release-process?view=azure-devops)
